observed_steps.name: Question 3
observed_steps.worked_solution:
The equation of motion for a particle of mass $m$ moving with forced harmonic motion without damping under the action of a spring with spring constant $k$ and external force $F(t)$ is given by

$$
m{y}^{″}=-ky+F(t).
$$

Substituting our values for $m$ and $F(t)$ gives

$$
0.5{y}^{″}=-ky-2\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t).
$$

Simplifying and rearranging the above equation, we get

$$
{y}^{″}+2ky=-4\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t).
$$

The complementary solution ${y}_{c}$ here represents simple harmonic motion, and it can be written as

$$
{y}_{c}=A\operatorname{cos}⁡\omega t+B\operatorname{sin}⁡\omega t,
$$

where $A$ and $B$ are arbitrary constants of integration, and $\omega $ is the system's internal frequency.

In our case,

$$
{\omega }^{2}=2k\,⟹\,k=\frac{1}{2}{\omega }^{2}.
$$

The oscillator experiences resonance when the frequency of the external periodic force $f(t)=-4\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t),$ which is $4,$ is equal to the frequency of the complementary solution $\omega .$

Therefore,

$$
k=\frac{1}{2}{\omega }^{2}=\frac{1}{2}\cdot {4}^{2}=8\,{\text{kg/s}}^{2}.
$$

The external force is $f(t)=8\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)-6\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t),$ which is sinusoidal with frequency $4.$ Therefore,
$\omega =4.$

The complementary solution for the associated simple harmonic motion equation can be written in three different forms:

1\. ${y}_{c}=R\operatorname{cos}⁡(\omega t+ϕ)=R\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t+ϕ)$

2\. ${y}_{c}=R\operatorname{sin}⁡(\omega t+ϕ)=R\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t+ϕ)$

3\. ${y}_{c}=A\operatorname{cos}⁡\omega t+B\operatorname{sin}⁡\omega t=A\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)$

$$
{y}_{p}(t)=t(C\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)+D\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)).
$$

By substituting the particular solution and $\omega =4$ into the differential equation, ${y}^{″}+{\omega }^{2}y=f(t),$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}[8(D-2Ct)\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)-8(C+2Dt)\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)]+16t(C\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)+D\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)) & =8\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)-6\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t) \\ 8D\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)-8C\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t) & =8\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)-6\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)\end{aligned}
$$

Equating coefficients, $C=\frac{3}{4}$ and $D=1.$ 

So, the particular solution is

$$
{y}_{p}(t)=\frac{3}{4}t\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)+t\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t).
$$

Finally, then, the general solution is given by the sum of the complementary and particular solutions. So, it can be written in any of the following forms:

question.name: Question 5
question.problem:
A particle is moving with forced harmonic motion without damping. The particle is acted on by an external periodic force
$f(t)=8\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)-6\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t).$
Assuming the system experiences resonance, which of the following could be used to represent the general solution for the position $y(t)?$

I. $y=R\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t+ϕ)+\frac{3}{4}t\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)+t\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)$

II. $y=R\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t+ϕ)+\frac{3}{4}t\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)+t\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)$

III. $y=A\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)+\frac{3}{4}t\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)+t\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)$

Note that $A,$ $B,$ $R,$ and $ϕ$ are constants.
question.worked_solution:
Because the motion is undamped and the system experiences resonance, the forcing frequency equals the natural frequency $\omega .$

The external force is $f(t)=8\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)-6\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t),$ which is sinusoidal with frequency $4.$ Therefore,
$\omega =4.$

The complementary solution for the associated simple harmonic motion equation can be written in three different forms:

1\. ${y}_{c}=R\operatorname{cos}⁡(\omega t+ϕ)=R\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t+ϕ)$

2\. ${y}_{c}=R\operatorname{sin}⁡(\omega t+ϕ)=R\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t+ϕ)$

3\. ${y}_{c}=A\operatorname{cos}⁡\omega t+B\operatorname{sin}⁡\omega t=A\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)$

At resonance, a sinusoidal trial at frequency $\omega $ duplicates the complementary solution, so we multiply by $t$ and take a resonant particular solution of the form

$$
{y}_{p}(t)=t(C\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)+D\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)).
$$

By substituting the particular solution and $\omega =4$ into the differential equation, ${y}^{″}+{\omega }^{2}y=f(t),$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}[8(D-2Ct)\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)-8(C+2Dt)\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)]+16t(C\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)+D\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)) & =8\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)-6\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t) \\ 8D\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)-8C\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t) & =8\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)-6\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)\end{aligned}
$$

Equating coefficients, $C=\frac{3}{4}$ and $D=1.$ 

So, the particular solution is

$$
{y}_{p}(t)=\frac{3}{4}t\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)+t\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t).
$$

Finally, then, the general solution is given by the sum of the complementary and particular solutions. So, it can be written in any of the following forms:

1\. $y=R\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t+ϕ)+\frac{3}{4}t\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)+t\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)$

2\. $y=R\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t+ϕ)+\frac{3}{4}t\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)+t\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)$

3\. $y=A\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)+\frac{3}{4}t\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)+t\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)$

Solutions I, II, and III match the forms above.
Therefore, the correct answer is "I, II, and III".

question.name: Question 1
question.problem:
The position $y(t),$ measured in meters, of a particle oscillating with periodically forced harmonic motion without damping is governed by the equation

$$
{y}^{″}+7y=-\operatorname{sin}⁡pt,
$$

where $t>0$ is the time, in seconds. Which value of the parameter $p$ causes the oscillator to resonate?
question.worked_solution:
The equation of forced harmonic motion without damping is

$$
{y}^{″}+{\omega }^{2}y=f(t).
$$

The complementary solution ${y}_{c}$ here represents simple harmonic motion, and it can be written as

$$
{y}_{c}=A\operatorname{cos}⁡\omega t+B\operatorname{sin}⁡\omega t,
$$

where $A$ and $B$ are arbitrary constants of integration.

In our case,

$$
{\omega }^{2}=7\,⟹\,\omega =\sqrt{7}.
$$

Thus, we have

$$
{y}_{c}=A\operatorname{cos}⁡\sqrt{7}t+B\operatorname{sin}⁡\sqrt{7}t.
$$

The oscillator experiences resonance when the frequency $p$ of the external periodic force $f(t)=-\operatorname{sin}⁡pt$ coincides with the frequency of the complementary solution, which is $\omega =\sqrt{7}.$

Therefore, the oscillator experiences resonance when $p=\sqrt{7}.$

question.name: Question 2
question.problem:
A particle is moving with forced harmonic motion without damping. The particle is acted on by an external periodic force
$f(t)=3\operatorname{sin}⁡t.$
Assuming the system experiences resonance, which of the following could be used to represent the general solution for the position $y(t)?$

I. $y=R\operatorname{cos}⁡(t+ϕ)-\frac{3}{2}t\operatorname{cos}⁡t$

II. $y=R\operatorname{sin}⁡(t+ϕ)+3t\operatorname{sin}⁡t$

III. $y=A\operatorname{cos}⁡t+B\operatorname{sin}⁡t-3t\operatorname{cos}⁡t+t\operatorname{sin}⁡t$

Note that $A,$ $B,$ $R,$ and $ϕ$ are constants.
question.worked_solution:
Because the motion is undamped and the system experiences resonance, the forcing frequency equals the natural frequency $\omega .$

The external force is $f(t)=3\operatorname{sin}⁡t,$ which is sinusoidal with frequency $1.$ Therefore,
$\omega =1.$

The complementary solution for the associated simple harmonic motion equation can be written in three different forms:

1\. ${y}_{c}=R\operatorname{cos}⁡(\omega t+ϕ)=R\operatorname{cos}⁡(t+ϕ)$

2\. ${y}_{c}=R\operatorname{sin}⁡(\omega t+ϕ)=R\operatorname{sin}⁡(t+ϕ)$

3\. ${y}_{c}=A\operatorname{cos}⁡\omega t+B\operatorname{sin}⁡\omega t=A\operatorname{cos}⁡t+B\operatorname{sin}⁡t$

At resonance, a sinusoidal trial at frequency $\omega $ duplicates the complementary solution, so we multiply by $t$ and take a resonant particular solution of the form

$$
{y}_{p}(t)=t(C\operatorname{cos}⁡t+D\operatorname{sin}⁡t).
$$

By substituting the particular solution and $\omega =1$ into the differential equation, ${y}^{″}+{\omega }^{2}y=f(t),$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}[(2D-Ct)\operatorname{cos}⁡t-(2C+Dt)\operatorname{sin}⁡(t)]+t(C\operatorname{cos}⁡t+D\operatorname{sin}⁡t) & =3\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ 2D\operatorname{cos}⁡t-2C\operatorname{sin}⁡(t) & =3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}
$$

Equating coefficients, $C=-\frac{3}{2}$ and $D=0.$ 

So, the particular solution is

$$
{y}_{p}(t)=-\frac{3}{2}t\operatorname{cos}⁡t.
$$

Finally, then, the general solution is given by the sum of the complementary and particular solutions. So, it can be written in any of the following forms:

1\. $y=R\operatorname{cos}⁡(t+ϕ)-\frac{3}{2}t\operatorname{cos}⁡t$

2\. $y=R\operatorname{sin}⁡(t+ϕ)-\frac{3}{2}t\operatorname{cos}⁡t$

3\. $y=A\operatorname{cos}⁡t+B\operatorname{sin}⁡t-\frac{3}{2}t\operatorname{cos}⁡t$

Only solution I matches the forms above.
Therefore, the correct answer is "I only".

question.name: Question 3
question.problem:
A particle of mass $0.5\,\text{kg}$ is attached to a massless spring. An external periodic force $F(t)=-2\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)\,\text{N}$ is applied to the particle.

The position of the particle is $y(t)$ (measured in meters), and $t>0$ is the time in seconds. If the particle moves with forced harmonic motion without damping and the system experiences resonance, what is the spring constant $k?$

$k=$
{{field-1}}${\text{kg/s}}^{2}$
question.worked_solution:
The equation of motion for a particle of mass $m$ moving with forced harmonic motion without damping under the action of a spring with spring constant $k$ and external force $F(t)$ is given by

$$
m{y}^{″}=-ky+F(t).
$$

Substituting our values for $m$ and $F(t)$ gives

$$
0.5{y}^{″}=-ky-2\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t).
$$

Simplifying and rearranging the above equation, we get

$$
{y}^{″}+2ky=-4\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t).
$$

The complementary solution ${y}_{c}$ here represents simple harmonic motion, and it can be written as

$$
{y}_{c}=A\operatorname{cos}⁡\omega t+B\operatorname{sin}⁡\omega t,
$$

where $A$ and $B$ are arbitrary constants of integration, and $\omega $ is the system's internal frequency.

In our case,

$$
{\omega }^{2}=2k\,⟹\,k=\frac{1}{2}{\omega }^{2}.
$$

The oscillator experiences resonance when the frequency of the external periodic force $f(t)=-4\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t),$ which is $4,$ is equal to the frequency of the complementary solution $\omega .$

Therefore,

$$
k=\frac{1}{2}{\omega }^{2}=\frac{1}{2}\cdot {4}^{2}=8\,{\text{kg/s}}^{2}.
$$

question.name: Question 5
question.problem:
A particle is moving with forced harmonic motion without damping. The particle is acted on by an external periodic force
$f(t)=8\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)-6\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t).$
Assuming the system experiences resonance, which of the following could be used to represent the general solution for the position $y(t)?$

I. $y=R\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t+ϕ)+\frac{3}{4}t\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)+t\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)$

II. $y=R\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t+ϕ)+\frac{3}{4}t\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)+t\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)$

III. $y=A\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)+\frac{3}{4}t\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)+t\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)$

Note that $A,$ $B,$ $R,$ and $ϕ$ are constants.
question.worked_solution:
Because the motion is undamped and the system experiences resonance, the forcing frequency equals the natural frequency $\omega .$

The external force is $f(t)=8\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)-6\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t),$ which is sinusoidal with frequency $4.$ Therefore,
$\omega =4.$

The complementary solution for the associated simple harmonic motion equation can be written in three different forms:

1\. ${y}_{c}=R\operatorname{cos}⁡(\omega t+ϕ)=R\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t+ϕ)$

2\. ${y}_{c}=R\operatorname{sin}⁡(\omega t+ϕ)=R\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t+ϕ)$

3\. ${y}_{c}=A\operatorname{cos}⁡\omega t+B\operatorname{sin}⁡\omega t=A\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)$

At resonance, a sinusoidal trial at frequency $\omega $ duplicates the complementary solution, so we multiply by $t$ and take a resonant particular solution of the form

$$
{y}_{p}(t)=t(C\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)+D\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)).
$$

By substituting the particular solution and $\omega =4$ into the differential equation, ${y}^{″}+{\omega }^{2}y=f(t),$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}[8(D-2Ct)\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)-8(C+2Dt)\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)]+16t(C\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)+D\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)) & =8\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)-6\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t) \\ 8D\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)-8C\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t) & =8\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)-6\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)\end{aligned}
$$

Equating coefficients, $C=\frac{3}{4}$ and $D=1.$ 

So, the particular solution is

$$
{y}_{p}(t)=\frac{3}{4}t\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)+t\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t).
$$

Finally, then, the general solution is given by the sum of the complementary and particular solutions. So, it can be written in any of the following forms:

1\. $y=R\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t+ϕ)+\frac{3}{4}t\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)+t\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)$

2\. $y=R\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t+ϕ)+\frac{3}{4}t\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)+t\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)$

3\. $y=A\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)+\frac{3}{4}t\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)+t\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)$

Solutions I, II, and III match the forms above.
Therefore, the correct answer is "I, II, and III".

questions.problem: What is the reciprocal of $131?$
questions.worked_solution:

$$
1÷131=\frac{1}{131}.
$$

questions.name: Question 5
questions.problem: The reciprocal of $-4\,\frac{1}{2}$ is{{field-1}}.
questions.worked_solution:
First, we write the number as a regular fraction:

$$
-4\,\frac{1}{2}=-\frac{4\cdot 2+1}{2}=-\frac{9}{2}
$$

Then, we flip the numerator and denominator, keeping the sign of the fraction. So the reciprocal of $-4\frac{1}{2}$ is $-\frac{2}{9}.$

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Finding the Reciprocal of a Mixed Number
canonical_examples.problem: Calculate the reciprocal of $-2\,\dfrac{1}{3}.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
First, we write the mixed number as an improper fraction:

$$
-2\,\dfrac{1}{3}=-\dfrac{2\cdot 3+1}{3}=-\dfrac{7}{3}
$$

Then, we flip the numerator and the denominator, keeping the negative sign. Therefore, the reciprocal of $-2\,\dfrac{1}{3}$ is $-\dfrac{3}{7}.$

canonical_examples.problem: What is the reciprocal of $0.4?$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
First, we must convert the decimal to a fraction. Doing this, we get

$$
0.4 = \dfrac{4}{10} = \dfrac{{\color{blue}{2}}}{{\color{red}{5}}}.
$$

Now, we flip the fraction, as before. So the reciprocal of $0.4$ is $\dfrac{{\color{red}{5}}}{{\color{blue}{2}}} = 2.5.$

tutorials.name: Introduction
tutorials.problem:
The **reciprocal** of a number is equal to ${\color{red}{1}}$ divided by the number. For example:

- the reciprocal of ${\color{blue}{2}}$ is equal to ${\color{red}{1}} \div {\color{blue}{2}} = \dfrac{1}{2}$

- the reciprocal of ${\color{blue}{3}}$ is equal to  ${\color{red}{1}} \div {\color{blue}{3}} = \dfrac{1}{3}$

- the reciprocal of $-{\color{blue}{7}}$ is equal to  ${\color{red}{1}} \div ({\color{blue}{-7}}) = -\dfrac{1}{7}$

The reciprocal of ${\color{blue}{1}}$ is  equal to  ${\color{red}{1}} \div {\color{blue}{1}} = 1.$ So the number $1$ is equal to its reciprocal. The same is true for $-1.$

The reciprocal of a number always has the same sign as the original number.

- If the number is positive, its reciprocal will be positive, while

- if the number is negative, its reciprocal is also negative.

tutorials.problem:

- the reciprocal of $- \dfrac {\color{red}{1}}{\color{blue}{7}}$ is $- \dfrac{{\color{blue}{7}}}{{\color{red}{1}}} = -7$

- the reciprocal of $\dfrac {\color{red}{2}} {\color{blue}{5}}$ is $\dfrac{{\color{blue}{5}}}{\color{red}{2}}$

- the reciprocal of $-\dfrac {\color{red}{4}} {\color{blue}{9}}$ is $-\dfrac{{\color{blue}{9}}}{\color{red}{4}}$

tutorials.name: The Product of a Number and Its Reciprocal
tutorials.problem:
The product of a number and its reciprocal is *always* equal to $1.$

For instance, the reciprocal of $2$ is $\dfrac{1}{2}.$ If we multiply these two numbers together, we get

$$
2 \cdot \dfrac{1}{2} = \dfrac{2\cdot 1}{2} = \dfrac{2}{2} = 1.
$$

 

Similarly, the product of $-10$ and its reciprocal $-\dfrac{1}{10}$ is

$$
(-10) \cdot \left(-\dfrac{1}{10}\right) = \dfrac{10\cdot 1}{10} = \dfrac{10}{10} = 1.
$$

 

In this case, we had a negative multiplied by a negative, which gave a positive.

tutorial.name: The Product of a Number and Its Reciprocal
tutorial.problem:
The product of a number and its reciprocal is *always* equal to $1.$

For instance, the reciprocal of $2$ is $\dfrac{1}{2}.$ If we multiply these two numbers together, we get

$$
2 \cdot \dfrac{1}{2} = \dfrac{2\cdot 1}{2} = \dfrac{2}{2} = 1.
$$

 

Similarly, the product of $-10$ and its reciprocal $-\dfrac{1}{10}$ is

$$
(-10) \cdot \left(-\dfrac{1}{10}\right) = \dfrac{10\cdot 1}{10} = \dfrac{10}{10} = 1.
$$

 

In this case, we had a negative multiplied by a negative, which gave a positive.

Question 4
?

What is the reciprocal of −113?

a
−1
b
113
c
−113
d
−13
e
13
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

We flip the numerator and denominator, keeping the sign of the fraction. So the reciprocal of −113 is −131=−13.

question.problem: The reciprocal of $-4\,\frac{1}{2}$ is{{field-1}}.
question.worked_solution:

$$
-4\,\frac{1}{2}=-\frac{4\cdot 2+1}{2}=-\frac{9}{2}
$$

Then, we flip the numerator and denominator, keeping the sign of the fraction. So the reciprocal of $-4\frac{1}{2}$ is $-\frac{2}{9}.$

Question 7

What is the reciprocal of 1058?

a
−85
b
885
c
185
d
−885
e
588
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we write the number as a regular fraction: 1058=10⋅8+58=858 Then, we flip the numerator and denominator, keeping the sign of the fraction. So the reciprocal of 1058 is 885.

question.name: Question 9
question.problem: What is the reciprocal of $7.5?$
question.worked_solution:
We first convert the decimal to a fraction. By doing this, we get

$$
7.5=\frac{75}{10}=\frac{15}{2}.
$$

Now, we flip the numerator and denominator. So the reciprocal of $7.5$ is $\frac{2}{15}.$

question.html:
Question 9
?

What is the reciprocal of 7.5?

a
−25
b
152
c
215
d
−215
e
52
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

We first convert the decimal to a fraction. By doing this, we get

7.5=7510=152.

Now, we flip the numerator and denominator. So the reciprocal of 7.5 is 215.

solution.reasoning: Since 7.5 = 15/2, its reciprocal is 2/15, matching option c. Their product is 1. No captured Math Academy answer or grade establishes its key for this question.

feedback.name: Question 9
feedback.problem: What is the reciprocal of $7.5?$
feedback.worked_solution:
We first convert the decimal to a fraction. By doing this, we get

$$
7.5=\frac{75}{10}=\frac{15}{2}.
$$

Now, we flip the numerator and denominator. So the reciprocal of $7.5$ is $\frac{2}{15}.$

questions.name: Question 1
questions.problem: A plate of mass $M$ occupies the region $D$ bounded by the curve $y=\sqrt{x},$ the line $x=1,$ and the $x$-axis. Its mass density at any point on the plate is given by $\lambda (x,y)=4My.$ Find the radius of gyration of the plate about the $x$-axis.
questions.worked_solution:
For a plane lamina in the shape of a region $D$ with mass $M$ and mass density function $\lambda (x,y),$ we have the following definitions:

- The radius of gyration ${R}_{x}$ about the $x$-axis is given by
${R}_{x}=\sqrt{\frac{{I}_{x}}{M}},$
where ${I}_{x}$ is the moment of inertia about the $x$-axis.

- The radius of gyration ${R}_{y}$ about the $y$-axis is given by
${R}_{y}=\sqrt{\frac{{I}_{y}}{M}},$
where ${I}_{y}$ is the moment of inertia about the $y$-axis.

- The radius of gyration ${R}_{0}$ about the origin is given by
${R}_{0}=\sqrt{\frac{{I}_{0}}{M}},$
where ${I}_{0}$ is the moment of inertia about the origin.

The moment of inertia about the $x$-axis is defined as

$$
{I}_{x}={∬}_{D}{y}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A,
$$

where $\lambda (x,y)$ is the mass density function. The region $D$ is a type I region with representation

$$
D=\{(x,y)\,:\,0\le x\le 1,\,\,0\le y\le \sqrt{x}\}.
$$

Hence, the moment of inertia about the $x$-axis is

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}_{x} & ={∬}_{D}{y}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{x}}{y}^{2}\cdot 4My\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & =4M{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{x}}{y}^{3}\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & =4M{\int }_{0}^{1}{[\frac{1}{4}{y}^{4}]}_{y=0}^{y=\sqrt{x}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =4M{\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{1}{4}{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =M{\int }_{0}^{1}{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =M{[\frac{1}{3}{x}^{3}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{M}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the radius of gyration about the $x$-axis is

$$
\begin{aligned}{R}_{x} & =\sqrt{\frac{{I}_{x}}{M}} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{M}{3}\cdot \frac{1}{M}} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{1}{3}} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 2
questions.problem:
A rectangular plate of mass $M$ and uniform mass density occupies the region
$D=\{(x,y)\,:\,0\le x\le 2,\,\,1\le y\le 3\}.$ Find the radius of gyration of the plate about the origin.
questions.worked_solution:
For a plane lamina in the shape of a region $D$ with mass $M$ and mass density function $\lambda (x,y),$ we have the following definitions:

- The radius of gyration ${R}_{x}$ about the $x$-axis is given by
${R}_{x}=\sqrt{\frac{{I}_{x}}{M}},$
where ${I}_{x}$ is the moment of inertia about the $x$-axis.

- The radius of gyration ${R}_{y}$ about the $y$-axis is given by
${R}_{y}=\sqrt{\frac{{I}_{y}}{M}},$
where ${I}_{y}$ is the moment of inertia about the $y$-axis.

- The radius of gyration ${R}_{0}$ about the origin is given by
${R}_{0}=\sqrt{\frac{{I}_{0}}{M}},$
where ${I}_{0}$ is the moment of inertia about the origin.

The moment of inertia about the origin is defined as

$$
{I}_{0}={∬}_{D}\lambda (x,y)({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\,\text{d}A,
$$

where $\lambda (x,y)$ is the mass density function.

The area of the rectangular plate $D$ is $A=2\cdot 2=4.$ Since the plate has uniform density, the mass density function is given by

$$
\lambda (x,y)=\frac{M}{A}=\frac{M}{4}.
$$

Therefore, the moment of inertia about the origin is

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}_{0} & ={∬}_{D}\lambda (x,y)({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\,\text{d}A \\  & =\frac{M}{4}{\int }_{1}^{3}{\int }_{0}^{2}{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{M}{4}{\int }_{1}^{3}{[\frac{1}{3}{x}^{3}+x{y}^{2}]}_{x=0}^{x=2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{M}{4}{\int }_{1}^{3}\frac{8}{3}+2{y}^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{M}{2}{\int }_{1}^{3}\frac{4}{3}+{y}^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{M}{2}{[\frac{4}{3}y+\frac{1}{3}{y}^{3}]}_{1}^{3} \\  & =\frac{M}{2}(4+9-(\frac{4}{3}+\frac{1}{3})) \\  & =\frac{M}{2}(13-\frac{5}{3}) \\  & =\frac{M}{2}\cdot \frac{34}{3} \\  & =\frac{17M}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally,

$$
{R}_{0}^{2}=\frac{17}{3}\,⇒\,{R}_{0}=\sqrt{\frac{17}{3}}.
$$

questions.name: Question 3
questions.problem:
A rectangular plate of mass $M$ and uniform mass density occupies the region
$D=\{(x,y)\,:\,0\le x\le 2,\,\,0\le y\le 3\}.$ Find the radius of gyration of the plate about the $y$-axis.
questions.worked_solution:
For a plane lamina in the shape of a region $D$ with mass $M$ and mass density function $\lambda (x,y),$ we have the following definitions:

- The radius of gyration ${R}_{x}$ about the $x$-axis is given by
${R}_{x}=\sqrt{\frac{{I}_{x}}{M}},$
where ${I}_{x}$ is the moment of inertia about the $x$-axis.

- The radius of gyration ${R}_{y}$ about the $y$-axis is given by
${R}_{y}=\sqrt{\frac{{I}_{y}}{M}},$
where ${I}_{y}$ is the moment of inertia about the $y$-axis.

- The radius of gyration ${R}_{0}$ about the origin is given by
${R}_{0}=\sqrt{\frac{{I}_{0}}{M}},$
where ${I}_{0}$ is the moment of inertia about the origin.

The moment of inertia about the $y$-axis is defined as

$$
{I}_{y}={∬}_{D}{x}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A,
$$

where $\lambda (x,y)$ is the mass density function.

The area of the rectangular plate $D$ is $A=2\cdot 3=6.$ Since the plate has uniform density, the mass density function is given by

$$
\lambda (x,y)=\frac{M}{A}=\frac{M}{6}.
$$

Therefore, the moment of inertia about the $y$-axis is

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}_{y} & ={∬}_{D}{x}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A \\  & =\frac{M}{6}{\int }_{0}^{3}{\int }_{0}^{2}{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{M}{6}{\int }_{0}^{3}{[\frac{1}{3}{x}^{3}]}_{0}^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{M}{6}{\int }_{0}^{3}\frac{1}{3}(8-0)\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{4M}{9}[y]_{0}^{3} \\  & =\frac{4M}{9}\cdot 3 \\  & =\frac{4M}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally,

$$
{R}_{y}^{2}=\frac{4}{3}\,⇒\,{R}_{y}=\sqrt{\frac{4}{3}}=\frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}.
$$

\begin{aligned}{I}_{0} & ={∬}_{D}\lambda (x,y)({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\,\text{d}A \\  & =\frac{M}{2}{\int }_{1}^{3}{\int }_{1}^{2}{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{M}{2}{\int }_{1}^{3}{[\frac{1}{3}{x}^{3}+x{y}^{2}]}_{x=1}^{x=2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{M}{2}{\int }_{1}^{3}(\frac{8}{3}+2{y}^{2}-\frac{1}{3}-{y}^{2})\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{M}{2}{\int }_{1}^{3}\frac{7}{3}+{y}^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{M}{2}{[\frac{7}{3}y+\frac{1}{3}{y}^{3}]}_{1}^{3} \\  & =\frac{M}{2}(7+9-\frac{7}{3}-\frac{1}{3}) \\  & =\frac{M}{2}\cdot \frac{40}{3} \\  & =\frac{20M}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally,

$$
{R}_{0}^{2}=\frac{20}{3}\,⇒\,{R}_{0}=\sqrt{\frac{20}{3}}=2\sqrt{\frac{5}{3}}.
$$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14151907/assets/5b8ddb36e814517af21d790374e1fb192141bd6ef0fd99e83a147c6ed5a62aea.png)

A plate of mass $M$ occupies the region $D$ in the first quadrant bounded by the circles ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=1,$ ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=4,$ and the coordinate axes, as shown above. Its mass density at any point is given by $\lambda (x,y)=\frac{3}{7}My.$ Find the radius of gyration of the plate about the $y$-axis.
questions.worked_solution:
For a plane lamina in the shape of a region $D$ with mass $M$ and mass density function $\lambda (x,y),$ we have the following definitions:

- The radius of gyration ${R}_{x}$ about the $x$-axis is given by
${R}_{x}=\sqrt{\frac{{I}_{x}}{M}},$
where ${I}_{x}$ is the moment of inertia about the $x$-axis.

- The radius of gyration ${R}_{y}$ about the $y$-axis is given by
${R}_{y}=\sqrt{\frac{{I}_{y}}{M}},$
where ${I}_{y}$ is the moment of inertia about the $y$-axis.

- The radius of gyration ${R}_{0}$ about the origin is given by
${R}_{0}=\sqrt{\frac{{I}_{0}}{M}},$
where ${I}_{0}$ is the moment of inertia about the origin.

In polar coordinates, the region occupied by the plate is given by

$$
D=\{(r,\theta )\,:\,1\le r\le 2,\,\,0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{2}\}.
$$

The moment of inertia about the $y$-axis, in polar coordinates, is defined as

$$
{I}_{y}={∬}_{D}\lambda (r,\theta ){r}^{3}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta ,
$$

where $\lambda (r,\theta )$ is the mass density function.

Also, the mass density in terms of polar coordinates is $\lambda (r,\theta )=\frac{3}{7}Mr\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .$
Therefore, the moment of inertia about the $y$-axis is

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}_{y} & ={∬}_{D}\lambda (r,\theta ){r}^{3}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{3}{7}M{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{1}^{2}{r}^{4}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{3}{7}M({\int }_{1}^{2}{r}^{4}\,\text{d}r)({\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta ) \\  & =\frac{3}{7}M\cdot \frac{1}{5}{r}^{5}{|}_{1}^{2}\cdot {[-\frac{{cos}^{3}⁡\theta }{3}]}_{0}^{\pi /2} \\  & =\frac{3}{7}M\cdot (\frac{32}{5}-\frac{1}{5})\cdot (-0+\frac{1}{3}) \\  & =\frac{3}{7}M\cdot \frac{31}{5}\cdot \frac{1}{3} \\  & =\frac{31M}{35}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the radius of gyration about the $x$-axis is

$$
\begin{aligned}{R}_{y} & =\sqrt{\frac{{I}_{y}}{M}} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{31M}{35}\cdot \frac{1}{M}} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{31}{35}}.\end{aligned}
$$

${R}_{0}=\sqrt{\frac{{I}_{0}}{M}},$
where ${I}_{0}$ is the moment of inertia about the origin.

$$
{I}_{x}={∬}_{D}{y}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A,

$$
D=\{(x,y)\,:\,0\le x\le 1,\,\,0\le y\le \sqrt{x}\}.
$$

Hence, the moment of inertia about the $x$-axis is

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}_{x} & ={∬}_{D}{y}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{x}}{y}^{2}\cdot 4My\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & =4M{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{x}}{y}^{3}\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & =4M{\int }_{0}^{1}{[\frac{1}{4}{y}^{4}]}_{y=0}^{y=\sqrt{x}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =4M{\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{1}{4}{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =M{\int }_{0}^{1}{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =M{[\frac{1}{3}{x}^{3}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{M}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{R}_{x} & =\sqrt{\frac{{I}_{x}}{M}} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{M}{3}\cdot \frac{1}{M}} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{1}{3}} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}.\end{aligned}
$$

  • The radius of gyration Rx about the x-axis is given by Rx=IxM, where Ix is the moment of inertia about the x-axis.

$$
{I}_{0}={∬}_{D}\lambda (x,y)({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\,\text{d}A,

$$
{I}_{0}={∬}_{D}\lambda (x,y)({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\,\text{d}A,

$$

$$

$$
{I}_{y}={∬}_{D}\lambda (r,\theta ){r}^{3}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta ,

A plate of mass $M$ occupies the region $D$ in the first quadrant bounded by the circles ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=1,$ ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=4,$ and the coordinate axes, as shown above. Its mass density at any point is given by $\lambda (x,y)=\frac{3}{7}My.$ Find the radius of gyration of the plate about the $y$-axis.
question.worked_solution:
For a plane lamina in the shape of a region $D$ with mass $M$ and mass density function $\lambda (x,y),$ we have the following definitions:

- The radius of gyration ${R}_{x}$ about the $x$-axis is given by
${R}_{x}=\sqrt{\frac{{I}_{x}}{M}},$
where ${I}_{x}$ is the moment of inertia about the $x$-axis.

- The radius of gyration ${R}_{y}$ about the $y$-axis is given by
${R}_{y}=\sqrt{\frac{{I}_{y}}{M}},$
where ${I}_{y}$ is the moment of inertia about the $y$-axis.

- The radius of gyration ${R}_{0}$ about the origin is given by
${R}_{0}=\sqrt{\frac{{I}_{0}}{M}},$
where ${I}_{0}$ is the moment of inertia about the origin.

In polar coordinates, the region occupied by the plate is given by

$$
D=\{(r,\theta )\,:\,1\le r\le 2,\,\,0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{2}\}.
$$

The moment of inertia about the $y$-axis, in polar coordinates, is defined as

$$
{I}_{y}={∬}_{D}\lambda (r,\theta ){r}^{3}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta ,
$$

where $\lambda (r,\theta )$ is the mass density function.

Also, the mass density in terms of polar coordinates is $\lambda (r,\theta )=\frac{3}{7}Mr\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .$
Therefore, the moment of inertia about the $y$-axis is

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}_{y} & ={∬}_{D}\lambda (r,\theta ){r}^{3}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{3}{7}M{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{1}^{2}{r}^{4}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{3}{7}M({\int }_{1}^{2}{r}^{4}\,\text{d}r)({\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta ) \\  & =\frac{3}{7}M\cdot \frac{1}{5}{r}^{5}{|}_{1}^{2}\cdot {[-\frac{{cos}^{3}⁡\theta }{3}]}_{0}^{\pi /2} \\  & =\frac{3}{7}M\cdot (\frac{32}{5}-\frac{1}{5})\cdot (-0+\frac{1}{3}) \\  & =\frac{3}{7}M\cdot \frac{31}{5}\cdot \frac{1}{3} \\  & =\frac{31M}{35}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the radius of gyration about the $x$-axis is

$$
\begin{aligned}{R}_{y} & =\sqrt{\frac{{I}_{y}}{M}} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{31M}{35}\cdot \frac{1}{M}} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{31}{35}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 5
?

A plate of mass M occupies the region D in the first quadrant bounded by the circles x2+y2=1, x2+y2=4, and the coordinate axes, as shown above. Its mass density at any point is given by λ(x,y)=37My. Find the radius of gyration of the plate about the y-axis.

a
 3135
b
 1115
c
 56
d
 1721
e
 710
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

For a plane lamina in the shape of a region D with mass M and mass density function λ(x,y), we have the following definitions:

  • The radius of gyration Rx about the x-axis is given by Rx=IxM, where Ix is the moment of inertia about the x-axis.

  • The radius of gyration Ry about the y-axis is given by Ry=IyM, where Iy is the moment of inertia about the y-axis.

  • The radius of gyration R0 about the origin is given by R0=I0M, where I0 is the moment of inertia about the origin.

In polar coordinates, the region occupied by the plate is given by D={(r,θ):1≤r≤2,0≤θ≤π2}.

The moment of inertia about the y-axis, in polar coordinates, is defined as

Iy=∬Dλ(r,θ)r3cos2⁡θdrdθ,

where λ(r,θ) is the mass density function.

Also, the mass density in terms of polar coordinates is λ(r,θ)=37Mrsin⁡θ. Therefore, the moment of inertia about the y-axis is

Iy=∬Dλ(r,θ)r3cos2⁡θdrdθ=37M∫0π/2∫12r4cos2⁡θsin⁡θdrdθ=37M(∫12r4dr)(∫0π/2cos2⁡θsin⁡θdθ)=37M⋅15r5|12⋅[−cos3⁡θ3]0π/2=37M⋅(325−15)⋅(−0+13)=37M⋅315⋅13=31M35.

Therefore, the radius of gyration about the x-axis is

Ry=IyM=31M35⋅1M=3135.

judgments.reasoning: The total mass is ∫₀¹∫₀^{√x}4My dy dx=M, and the moment of inertia about the x-axis is ∫₀¹∫₀^{√x}4My³ dy dx=M/3. Therefore R_x=√(I_x/M)=1/√3, option b. This agrees with the earlier answer, the submitted response graded Correct, and Math Academy's worked solution.

Uniform density is M/4. The mean squared distance from the origin is 4/3+13/3=17/3, so I₀=17M/3 and R₀=√(17/3), option a. This agrees with the earlier answer and Math Academy's worked solution. The recorded submission was instead √(13/3), option b, which omits the x² contribution; its Incorrect grade is consistent with the mathematics.

The uniform density is M/6. The moment of inertia about the y-axis is I_y=(M/6)∫₀³∫₀²x² dx dy=4M/3, giving R_y=√(I_y/M)=2/√3, option e. This agrees with the earlier answer, the submitted response graded Correct, and Math Academy's worked solution.

The uniform density is M/2. The mean squared distance from the origin is 7/3+13/3=20/3, so I₀=20M/3 and R₀=√(20/3)=2√(5/3), option e. This agrees with the earlier answer and Math Academy's worked solution. The recorded submission was instead √(17/5), option a, so its Incorrect grade is mathematically consistent.

In polar coordinates, I_y=(3M/7)(∫₁²r⁴ dr)(∫₀^{π/2}cos²θ sinθ dθ)=(3M/7)(31/5)(1/3)=31M/35. Thus R_y=√(31/35), option a, agreeing with the earlier answer, the Correct grade, and Math Academy's final equation. The worked solution's concluding prose mistakenly says x-axis; its calculation and final R_y equation correctly concern the y-axis.

question.name: Question 1
question.problem: A plate of mass $M$ occupies the region $D$ bounded by the curve $y=\sqrt{x},$ the line $x=1,$ and the $x$-axis. Its mass density at any point on the plate is given by $\lambda (x,y)=4My.$ Find the radius of gyration of the plate about the $x$-axis.
question.worked_solution:
For a plane lamina in the shape of a region $D$ with mass $M$ and mass density function $\lambda (x,y),$ we have the following definitions:

- The radius of gyration ${R}_{x}$ about the $x$-axis is given by
${R}_{x}=\sqrt{\frac{{I}_{x}}{M}},$
where ${I}_{x}$ is the moment of inertia about the $x$-axis.

- The radius of gyration ${R}_{y}$ about the $y$-axis is given by
${R}_{y}=\sqrt{\frac{{I}_{y}}{M}},$
where ${I}_{y}$ is the moment of inertia about the $y$-axis.

- The radius of gyration ${R}_{0}$ about the origin is given by
${R}_{0}=\sqrt{\frac{{I}_{0}}{M}},$
where ${I}_{0}$ is the moment of inertia about the origin.

The moment of inertia about the $x$-axis is defined as

$$
{I}_{x}={∬}_{D}{y}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A,
$$

where $\lambda (x,y)$ is the mass density function. The region $D$ is a type I region with representation

$$
D=\{(x,y)\,:\,0\le x\le 1,\,\,0\le y\le \sqrt{x}\}.
$$

Hence, the moment of inertia about the $x$-axis is

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}_{x} & ={∬}_{D}{y}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{x}}{y}^{2}\cdot 4My\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & =4M{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{x}}{y}^{3}\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & =4M{\int }_{0}^{1}{[\frac{1}{4}{y}^{4}]}_{y=0}^{y=\sqrt{x}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =4M{\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{1}{4}{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =M{\int }_{0}^{1}{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =M{[\frac{1}{3}{x}^{3}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{M}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the radius of gyration about the $x$-axis is

$$
\begin{aligned}{R}_{x} & =\sqrt{\frac{{I}_{x}}{M}} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{M}{3}\cdot \frac{1}{M}} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{1}{3}} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 1

A plate of mass M occupies the region D bounded by the curve y=x, the line x=1, and the x-axis. Its mass density at any point on the plate is given by λ(x,y)=4My. Find the radius of gyration of the plate about the x-axis.

a
23
b
13
c
35
d
1
e
12
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

For a plane lamina in the shape of a region D with mass M and mass density function λ(x,y), we have the following definitions:

  • The radius of gyration Rx about the x-axis is given by Rx=IxM, where Ix is the moment of inertia about the x-axis.

  • The radius of gyration Ry about the y-axis is given by Ry=IyM, where Iy is the moment of inertia about the y-axis.

  • The radius of gyration R0 about the origin is given by R0=I0M, where I0 is the moment of inertia about the origin.

The moment of inertia about the x-axis is defined as Ix=∬Dy2λ(x,y)dA, where λ(x,y) is the mass density function. The region D is a type I region with representation D={(x,y):0≤x≤1,0≤y≤x}.

For a plane lamina in the shape of a region $D$ with mass $M$ and mass density function $\lambda (x,y),$ we have the following definitions:

- The radius of gyration ${R}_{x}$ about the $x$-axis is given by
${R}_{x}=\sqrt{\frac{{I}_{x}}{M}},$
where ${I}_{x}$ is the moment of inertia about the $x$-axis.

- The radius of gyration ${R}_{y}$ about the $y$-axis is given by
${R}_{y}=\sqrt{\frac{{I}_{y}}{M}},$
where ${I}_{y}$ is the moment of inertia about the $y$-axis.

- The radius of gyration ${R}_{0}$ about the origin is given by
${R}_{0}=\sqrt{\frac{{I}_{0}}{M}},$
where ${I}_{0}$ is the moment of inertia about the origin.

The moment of inertia about the $x$-axis is defined as

$$
{I}_{x}={∬}_{D}{y}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A,
$$

where $\lambda (x,y)$ is the mass density function. The region $D$ is a type I region with representation

$$
D=\{(x,y)\,:\,0\le x\le 1,\,\,0\le y\le \sqrt{x}\}.
$$

Hence, the moment of inertia about the $x$-axis is

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}_{x} & ={∬}_{D}{y}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{x}}{y}^{2}\cdot 4My\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & =4M{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{x}}{y}^{3}\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & =4M{\int }_{0}^{1}{[\frac{1}{4}{y}^{4}]}_{y=0}^{y=\sqrt{x}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =4M{\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{1}{4}{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =M{\int }_{0}^{1}{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =M{[\frac{1}{3}{x}^{3}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{M}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the radius of gyration about the $x$-axis is

$$
\begin{aligned}{R}_{x} & =\sqrt{\frac{{I}_{x}}{M}} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{M}{3}\cdot \frac{1}{M}} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{1}{3}} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}.\end{aligned}
$$

A plate of mass M occupies the region D bounded by the curve y=x, the line x=1, and the x-axis. Its mass density at any point on the plate is given by λ(x,y)=4My. Find the radius of gyration of the plate about the x-axis.

Correct
EXPLANATION

For a plane lamina in the shape of a region D with mass M and mass density function λ(x,y), we have the following definitions:

  • The radius of gyration Rx about the x-axis is given by Rx=IxM, where Ix is the moment of inertia about the x-axis.

  • The radius of gyration Ry about the y-axis is given by Ry=IyM, where Iy is the moment of inertia about the y-axis.

  • The radius of gyration R0 about the origin is given by R0=I0M, where I0 is the moment of inertia about the origin.

The moment of inertia about the x-axis is defined as Ix=∬Dy2λ(x,y)dA, where λ(x,y) is the mass density function. The region D is a type I region with representation D={(x,y):0≤x≤1,0≤y≤x}.

Hence, the moment of inertia about the x-axis is Ix=∬Dy2λ(x,y)dA=∫01∫0xy2⋅4Mydydx=4M∫01∫0xy3dydx=4M∫01[14y4]y=0y=xdx=4M∫0114x2dx=M∫01x2dx=M[13x3]01=M3.

Therefore, the radius of gyration about the x-axis is Rx=IxM=M3⋅1M=13=13.

Thus the radius of gyration is √(I_x/M)=1/√3, option b. The mathematics is resolved, but no Math Academy answer-key evidence was captured.

Question 1
?

A plate of mass M occupies the region D bounded by the curve y=x, the line x=1, and the x-axis. Its mass density at any point on the plate is given by λ(x,y)=4My. Find the radius of gyration of the plate about the x-axis.

a
23
b
13
c
35
d
1
e
12
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

For a plane lamina in the shape of a region D with mass M and mass density function λ(x,y), we have the following definitions:

  • The radius of gyration Rx about the x-axis is given by Rx=IxM, where Ix is the moment of inertia about the x-axis.

  • The radius of gyration Ry about the y-axis is given by Ry=IyM, where Iy is the moment of inertia about the y-axis.

  • The radius of gyration R0 about the origin is given by R0=I0M, where I0 is the moment of inertia about the origin.

The moment of inertia about the x-axis is defined as Ix=∬Dy2λ(x,y)dA, where λ(x,y) is the mass density function. The region D is a type I region with representation D={(x,y):0≤x≤1,0≤y≤x}.

Hence, the moment of inertia about the x-axis is Ix=∬Dy2λ(x,y)dA=∫01∫0xy2⋅4Mydydx=4M∫01∫0xy3dydx=4M∫01[14y4]y=0y=xdx=4M∫0114x2dx=M∫01x2dx=M[13x3]01=M3.

Therefore, the radius of gyration about the x-axis is Rx=IxM=M3⋅1M=13=13.

question.name: Question 2
question.problem:
A rectangular plate of mass $M$ and uniform mass density occupies the region
$D=\{(x,y)\,:\,0\le x\le 2,\,\,1\le y\le 3\}.$ Find the radius of gyration of the plate about the origin.
question.worked_solution:
For a plane lamina in the shape of a region $D$ with mass $M$ and mass density function $\lambda (x,y),$ we have the following definitions:

- The radius of gyration ${R}_{x}$ about the $x$-axis is given by
${R}_{x}=\sqrt{\frac{{I}_{x}}{M}},$
where ${I}_{x}$ is the moment of inertia about the $x$-axis.

- The radius of gyration ${R}_{y}$ about the $y$-axis is given by
${R}_{y}=\sqrt{\frac{{I}_{y}}{M}},$
where ${I}_{y}$ is the moment of inertia about the $y$-axis.

- The radius of gyration ${R}_{0}$ about the origin is given by
${R}_{0}=\sqrt{\frac{{I}_{0}}{M}},$
where ${I}_{0}$ is the moment of inertia about the origin.

The moment of inertia about the origin is defined as

$$
{I}_{0}={∬}_{D}\lambda (x,y)({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\,\text{d}A,
$$

where $\lambda (x,y)$ is the mass density function.

The area of the rectangular plate $D$ is $A=2\cdot 2=4.$ Since the plate has uniform density, the mass density function is given by

$$
\lambda (x,y)=\frac{M}{A}=\frac{M}{4}.
$$

Therefore, the moment of inertia about the origin is

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}_{0} & ={∬}_{D}\lambda (x,y)({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\,\text{d}A \\  & =\frac{M}{4}{\int }_{1}^{3}{\int }_{0}^{2}{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{M}{4}{\int }_{1}^{3}{[\frac{1}{3}{x}^{3}+x{y}^{2}]}_{x=0}^{x=2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{M}{4}{\int }_{1}^{3}\frac{8}{3}+2{y}^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{M}{2}{\int }_{1}^{3}\frac{4}{3}+{y}^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{M}{2}{[\frac{4}{3}y+\frac{1}{3}{y}^{3}]}_{1}^{3} \\  & =\frac{M}{2}(4+9-(\frac{4}{3}+\frac{1}{3})) \\  & =\frac{M}{2}(13-\frac{5}{3}) \\  & =\frac{M}{2}\cdot \frac{34}{3} \\  & =\frac{17M}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally,

$$
{R}_{0}^{2}=\frac{17}{3}\,⇒\,{R}_{0}=\sqrt{\frac{17}{3}}.
$$

  • The radius of gyration R0 about the origin is given by R0=I0M, where I0 is the moment of inertia about the origin.

The moment of inertia about the origin is defined as

I0=∬Dλ(x,y)(x2+y2)dA,

I0=∬Dλ(x,y)(x2+y2)dA=M4∫13∫02x2+y2dxdy=M4∫13[13x3+xy2]x=0x=2dy=M4∫1383+2y2dy=M2∫1343+y2dy=M2[43y+13y3]13=M2(4+9−(43+13))=M2(13−53)=M2⋅343=17M3.

R02=173⇒R0=173.

last_observation.worked_solution:
For a plane lamina in the shape of a region $D$ with mass $M$ and mass density function $\lambda (x,y),$ we have the following definitions:

- The radius of gyration ${R}_{x}$ about the $x$-axis is given by
${R}_{x}=\sqrt{\frac{{I}_{x}}{M}},$
where ${I}_{x}$ is the moment of inertia about the $x$-axis.

- The radius of gyration ${R}_{y}$ about the $y$-axis is given by
${R}_{y}=\sqrt{\frac{{I}_{y}}{M}},$
where ${I}_{y}$ is the moment of inertia about the $y$-axis.

- The radius of gyration ${R}_{0}$ about the origin is given by
${R}_{0}=\sqrt{\frac{{I}_{0}}{M}},$
where ${I}_{0}$ is the moment of inertia about the origin.

The moment of inertia about the origin is defined as

$$
{I}_{0}={∬}_{D}\lambda (x,y)({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\,\text{d}A,
$$

where $\lambda (x,y)$ is the mass density function.

The area of the rectangular plate $D$ is $A=2\cdot 2=4.$ Since the plate has uniform density, the mass density function is given by

$$
\lambda (x,y)=\frac{M}{A}=\frac{M}{4}.
$$

Therefore, the moment of inertia about the origin is

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}_{0} & ={∬}_{D}\lambda (x,y)({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\,\text{d}A \\  & =\frac{M}{4}{\int }_{1}^{3}{\int }_{0}^{2}{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{M}{4}{\int }_{1}^{3}{[\frac{1}{3}{x}^{3}+x{y}^{2}]}_{x=0}^{x=2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{M}{4}{\int }_{1}^{3}\frac{8}{3}+2{y}^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{M}{2}{\int }_{1}^{3}\frac{4}{3}+{y}^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{M}{2}{[\frac{4}{3}y+\frac{1}{3}{y}^{3}]}_{1}^{3} \\  & =\frac{M}{2}(4+9-(\frac{4}{3}+\frac{1}{3})) \\  & =\frac{M}{2}(13-\frac{5}{3}) \\  & =\frac{M}{2}\cdot \frac{34}{3} \\  & =\frac{17M}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally,

$$
{R}_{0}^{2}=\frac{17}{3}\,⇒\,{R}_{0}=\sqrt{\frac{17}{3}}.
$$

EXPLANATION

For a plane lamina in the shape of a region D with mass M and mass density function λ(x,y), we have the following definitions:

  • The radius of gyration Rx about the x-axis is given by Rx=IxM, where Ix is the moment of inertia about the x-axis.

  • The radius of gyration Ry about the y-axis is given by Ry=IyM, where Iy is the moment of inertia about the y-axis.

  • The radius of gyration R0 about the origin is given by R0=I0M, where I0 is the moment of inertia about the origin.

The moment of inertia about the origin is defined as

I0=∬Dλ(x,y)(x2+y2)dA,

where λ(x,y) is the mass density function.

The area of the rectangular plate D is A=2⋅2=4. Since the plate has uniform density, the mass density function is given by λ(x,y)=MA=M4.

Therefore, the moment of inertia about the origin is

I0=∬Dλ(x,y)(x2+y2)dA=M4∫13∫02x2+y2dxdy=M4∫13[13x3+xy2]x=0x=2dy=M4∫1383+2y2dy=M2∫1343+y2dy=M2[43y+13y3]13=M2(4+9−(43+13))=M2(13−53)=M2⋅343=17M3.

R02=173⇒R0=173.

question.problem:
A rectangular plate of mass $M$ and uniform mass density occupies the region
$D=\{(x,y)\,:\,0\le x\le 2,\,\,0\le y\le 3\}.$ Find the radius of gyration of the plate about the $y$-axis.
question.worked_solution:
For a plane lamina in the shape of a region $D$ with mass $M$ and mass density function $\lambda (x,y),$ we have the following definitions:

- The radius of gyration ${R}_{x}$ about the $x$-axis is given by
${R}_{x}=\sqrt{\frac{{I}_{x}}{M}},$
where ${I}_{x}$ is the moment of inertia about the $x$-axis.

- The radius of gyration ${R}_{y}$ about the $y$-axis is given by
${R}_{y}=\sqrt{\frac{{I}_{y}}{M}},$
where ${I}_{y}$ is the moment of inertia about the $y$-axis.

- The radius of gyration ${R}_{0}$ about the origin is given by
${R}_{0}=\sqrt{\frac{{I}_{0}}{M}},$
where ${I}_{0}$ is the moment of inertia about the origin.

The moment of inertia about the $y$-axis is defined as

$$
{I}_{y}={∬}_{D}{x}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A,
$$

where $\lambda (x,y)$ is the mass density function.

The area of the rectangular plate $D$ is $A=2\cdot 3=6.$ Since the plate has uniform density, the mass density function is given by

$$
\lambda (x,y)=\frac{M}{A}=\frac{M}{6}.
$$

Therefore, the moment of inertia about the $y$-axis is

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}_{y} & ={∬}_{D}{x}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A \\  & =\frac{M}{6}{\int }_{0}^{3}{\int }_{0}^{2}{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{M}{6}{\int }_{0}^{3}{[\frac{1}{3}{x}^{3}]}_{0}^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{M}{6}{\int }_{0}^{3}\frac{1}{3}(8-0)\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{4M}{9}[y]_{0}^{3} \\  & =\frac{4M}{9}\cdot 3 \\  & =\frac{4M}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally,

$$
{R}_{y}^{2}=\frac{4}{3}\,⇒\,{R}_{y}=\sqrt{\frac{4}{3}}=\frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}.
$$

A rectangular plate of mass M and uniform mass density occupies the region D={(x,y):0≤x≤2,0≤y≤3}. Find the radius of gyration of the plate about the y-axis.

EXPLANATION

For a plane lamina in the shape of a region D with mass M and mass density function λ(x,y), we have the following definitions:

  • The radius of gyration Rx about the x-axis is given by Rx=IxM, where Ix is the moment of inertia about the x-axis.

  • The radius of gyration Ry about the y-axis is given by Ry=IyM, where Iy is the moment of inertia about the y-axis.

  • The radius of gyration R0 about the origin is given by R0=I0M, where I0 is the moment of inertia about the origin.

The moment of inertia about the y-axis is defined as

Iy=∬Dx2λ(x,y)dA,

where λ(x,y) is the mass density function.

The area of the rectangular plate D is A=2⋅3=6. Since the plate has uniform density, the mass density function is given by λ(x,y)=MA=M6.

Therefore, the moment of inertia about the y-axis is

Iy=∬Dx2λ(x,y)dA=M6∫03∫02x2dxdy=M6∫03[13x3]02dy=M6∫0313(8−0)dy=4M9[y]03=4M9⋅3=4M3.

Ry2=43⇒Ry=43=23.

feedback.name: Question 3
feedback.problem:
A rectangular plate of mass $M$ and uniform mass density occupies the region
$D=\{(x,y)\,:\,0\le x\le 2,\,\,0\le y\le 3\}.$ Find the radius of gyration of the plate about the $y$-axis.
feedback.worked_solution:
For a plane lamina in the shape of a region $D$ with mass $M$ and mass density function $\lambda (x,y),$ we have the following definitions:

- The radius of gyration ${R}_{x}$ about the $x$-axis is given by
${R}_{x}=\sqrt{\frac{{I}_{x}}{M}},$
where ${I}_{x}$ is the moment of inertia about the $x$-axis.

- The radius of gyration ${R}_{y}$ about the $y$-axis is given by
${R}_{y}=\sqrt{\frac{{I}_{y}}{M}},$
where ${I}_{y}$ is the moment of inertia about the $y$-axis.

- The radius of gyration ${R}_{0}$ about the origin is given by
${R}_{0}=\sqrt{\frac{{I}_{0}}{M}},$
where ${I}_{0}$ is the moment of inertia about the origin.

The moment of inertia about the $y$-axis is defined as

$$
{I}_{y}={∬}_{D}{x}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A,
$$

where $\lambda (x,y)$ is the mass density function.

The area of the rectangular plate $D$ is $A=2\cdot 3=6.$ Since the plate has uniform density, the mass density function is given by

$$
\lambda (x,y)=\frac{M}{A}=\frac{M}{6}.
$$

Therefore, the moment of inertia about the $y$-axis is

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}_{y} & ={∬}_{D}{x}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A \\  & =\frac{M}{6}{\int }_{0}^{3}{\int }_{0}^{2}{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{M}{6}{\int }_{0}^{3}{[\frac{1}{3}{x}^{3}]}_{0}^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{M}{6}{\int }_{0}^{3}\frac{1}{3}(8-0)\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{4M}{9}[y]_{0}^{3} \\  & =\frac{4M}{9}\cdot 3 \\  & =\frac{4M}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally,

$$
{R}_{y}^{2}=\frac{4}{3}\,⇒\,{R}_{y}=\sqrt{\frac{4}{3}}=\frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}.
$$

question.name: Question 4
question.problem:
A rectangular plate of mass $M$ and uniform mass density occupies the region
$D=\{(x,y)\,:\,1\le x\le 2,\,\,1\le y\le 3\}.$ Find the radius of gyration of the plate about the origin.
question.worked_solution:
For a plane lamina in the shape of a region $D$ with mass $M$ and mass density function $\lambda (x,y),$ we have the following definitions:

- The radius of gyration ${R}_{x}$ about the $x$-axis is given by
${R}_{x}=\sqrt{\frac{{I}_{x}}{M}},$
where ${I}_{x}$ is the moment of inertia about the $x$-axis.

- The radius of gyration ${R}_{y}$ about the $y$-axis is given by
${R}_{y}=\sqrt{\frac{{I}_{y}}{M}},$
where ${I}_{y}$ is the moment of inertia about the $y$-axis.

- The radius of gyration ${R}_{0}$ about the origin is given by
${R}_{0}=\sqrt{\frac{{I}_{0}}{M}},$
where ${I}_{0}$ is the moment of inertia about the origin.

The moment of inertia about the origin is defined as

$$
{I}_{0}={∬}_{D}\lambda (x,y)({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\,\text{d}A,
$$

where $\lambda (x,y)$ is the mass density function.

The area of the rectangular plate $D$ is $A=1\cdot 2=2.$ Since the plate has uniform density, the mass density function is given by

$$
\lambda (x,y)=\frac{M}{A}=\frac{M}{2}.
$$

Therefore, the moment of inertia about the origin is

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}_{0} & ={∬}_{D}\lambda (x,y)({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\,\text{d}A \\  & =\frac{M}{2}{\int }_{1}^{3}{\int }_{1}^{2}{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{M}{2}{\int }_{1}^{3}{[\frac{1}{3}{x}^{3}+x{y}^{2}]}_{x=1}^{x=2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{M}{2}{\int }_{1}^{3}(\frac{8}{3}+2{y}^{2}-\frac{1}{3}-{y}^{2})\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{M}{2}{\int }_{1}^{3}\frac{7}{3}+{y}^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{M}{2}{[\frac{7}{3}y+\frac{1}{3}{y}^{3}]}_{1}^{3} \\  & =\frac{M}{2}(7+9-\frac{7}{3}-\frac{1}{3}) \\  & =\frac{M}{2}\cdot \frac{40}{3} \\  & =\frac{20M}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally,

$$
{R}_{0}^{2}=\frac{20}{3}\,⇒\,{R}_{0}=\sqrt{\frac{20}{3}}=2\sqrt{\frac{5}{3}}.
$$

A rectangular plate of mass M and uniform mass density occupies the region D={(x,y):1≤x≤2,1≤y≤3}. Find the radius of gyration of the plate about the origin.

last_observation.worked_solution:
For a plane lamina in the shape of a region $D$ with mass $M$ and mass density function $\lambda (x,y),$ we have the following definitions:

- The radius of gyration ${R}_{x}$ about the $x$-axis is given by
${R}_{x}=\sqrt{\frac{{I}_{x}}{M}},$
where ${I}_{x}$ is the moment of inertia about the $x$-axis.

- The radius of gyration ${R}_{y}$ about the $y$-axis is given by
${R}_{y}=\sqrt{\frac{{I}_{y}}{M}},$
where ${I}_{y}$ is the moment of inertia about the $y$-axis.

- The radius of gyration ${R}_{0}$ about the origin is given by
${R}_{0}=\sqrt{\frac{{I}_{0}}{M}},$
where ${I}_{0}$ is the moment of inertia about the origin.

The moment of inertia about the origin is defined as

$$
{I}_{0}={∬}_{D}\lambda (x,y)({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\,\text{d}A,
$$

where $\lambda (x,y)$ is the mass density function.

The area of the rectangular plate $D$ is $A=1\cdot 2=2.$ Since the plate has uniform density, the mass density function is given by

$$
\lambda (x,y)=\frac{M}{A}=\frac{M}{2}.
$$

Therefore, the moment of inertia about the origin is

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}_{0} & ={∬}_{D}\lambda (x,y)({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\,\text{d}A \\  & =\frac{M}{2}{\int }_{1}^{3}{\int }_{1}^{2}{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{M}{2}{\int }_{1}^{3}{[\frac{1}{3}{x}^{3}+x{y}^{2}]}_{x=1}^{x=2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{M}{2}{\int }_{1}^{3}(\frac{8}{3}+2{y}^{2}-\frac{1}{3}-{y}^{2})\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{M}{2}{\int }_{1}^{3}\frac{7}{3}+{y}^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{M}{2}{[\frac{7}{3}y+\frac{1}{3}{y}^{3}]}_{1}^{3} \\  & =\frac{M}{2}(7+9-\frac{7}{3}-\frac{1}{3}) \\  & =\frac{M}{2}\cdot \frac{40}{3} \\  & =\frac{20M}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally,

$$
{R}_{0}^{2}=\frac{20}{3}\,⇒\,{R}_{0}=\sqrt{\frac{20}{3}}=2\sqrt{\frac{5}{3}}.
$$

Question 4

A rectangular plate of mass M and uniform mass density occupies the region D={(x,y):1≤x≤2,1≤y≤3}. Find the radius of gyration of the plate about the origin.

EXPLANATION

For a plane lamina in the shape of a region D with mass M and mass density function λ(x,y), we have the following definitions:

  • The radius of gyration Rx about the x-axis is given by Rx=IxM, where Ix is the moment of inertia about the x-axis.

  • The radius of gyration Ry about the y-axis is given by Ry=IyM, where Iy is the moment of inertia about the y-axis.

  • The radius of gyration R0 about the origin is given by R0=I0M, where I0 is the moment of inertia about the origin.

The moment of inertia about the origin is defined as

I0=∬Dλ(x,y)(x2+y2)dA,

where λ(x,y) is the mass density function.

The area of the rectangular plate D is A=1⋅2=2. Since the plate has uniform density, the mass density function is given by λ(x,y)=MA=M2.

Therefore, the moment of inertia about the origin is

I0=∬Dλ(x,y)(x2+y2)dA=M2∫13∫12x2+y2dxdy=M2∫13[13x3+xy2]x=1x=2dy=M2∫13(83+2y2−13−y2)dy=M2∫1373+y2dy=M2[73y+13y3]13=M2(7+9−73−13)=M2⋅403=20M3.

Finally,

R02=203⇒R0=203=253.

feedback.name: Question 4
feedback.problem:
A rectangular plate of mass $M$ and uniform mass density occupies the region
$D=\{(x,y)\,:\,1\le x\le 2,\,\,1\le y\le 3\}.$ Find the radius of gyration of the plate about the origin.
feedback.worked_solution:
For a plane lamina in the shape of a region $D$ with mass $M$ and mass density function $\lambda (x,y),$ we have the following definitions:

- The radius of gyration ${R}_{x}$ about the $x$-axis is given by
${R}_{x}=\sqrt{\frac{{I}_{x}}{M}},$
where ${I}_{x}$ is the moment of inertia about the $x$-axis.

- The radius of gyration ${R}_{y}$ about the $y$-axis is given by
${R}_{y}=\sqrt{\frac{{I}_{y}}{M}},$
where ${I}_{y}$ is the moment of inertia about the $y$-axis.

- The radius of gyration ${R}_{0}$ about the origin is given by
${R}_{0}=\sqrt{\frac{{I}_{0}}{M}},$
where ${I}_{0}$ is the moment of inertia about the origin.

The moment of inertia about the origin is defined as

$$
{I}_{0}={∬}_{D}\lambda (x,y)({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\,\text{d}A,
$$

where $\lambda (x,y)$ is the mass density function.

The area of the rectangular plate $D$ is $A=1\cdot 2=2.$ Since the plate has uniform density, the mass density function is given by

$$
\lambda (x,y)=\frac{M}{A}=\frac{M}{2}.
$$

Therefore, the moment of inertia about the origin is

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}_{0} & ={∬}_{D}\lambda (x,y)({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\,\text{d}A \\  & =\frac{M}{2}{\int }_{1}^{3}{\int }_{1}^{2}{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{M}{2}{\int }_{1}^{3}{[\frac{1}{3}{x}^{3}+x{y}^{2}]}_{x=1}^{x=2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{M}{2}{\int }_{1}^{3}(\frac{8}{3}+2{y}^{2}-\frac{1}{3}-{y}^{2})\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{M}{2}{\int }_{1}^{3}\frac{7}{3}+{y}^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{M}{2}{[\frac{7}{3}y+\frac{1}{3}{y}^{3}]}_{1}^{3} \\  & =\frac{M}{2}(7+9-\frac{7}{3}-\frac{1}{3}) \\  & =\frac{M}{2}\cdot \frac{40}{3} \\  & =\frac{20M}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally,

$$
{R}_{0}^{2}=\frac{20}{3}\,⇒\,{R}_{0}=\sqrt{\frac{20}{3}}=2\sqrt{\frac{5}{3}}.
$$

question.name: Question 5
question.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14151907/assets/5b8ddb36e814517af21d790374e1fb192141bd6ef0fd99e83a147c6ed5a62aea.png)

A plate of mass $M$ occupies the region $D$ in the first quadrant bounded by the circles ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=1,$ ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=4,$ and the coordinate axes, as shown above. Its mass density at any point is given by $\lambda (x,y)=\frac{3}{7}My.$ Find the radius of gyration of the plate about the $y$-axis.
question.worked_solution:
For a plane lamina in the shape of a region $D$ with mass $M$ and mass density function $\lambda (x,y),$ we have the following definitions:

- The radius of gyration ${R}_{x}$ about the $x$-axis is given by
${R}_{x}=\sqrt{\frac{{I}_{x}}{M}},$
where ${I}_{x}$ is the moment of inertia about the $x$-axis.

- The radius of gyration ${R}_{y}$ about the $y$-axis is given by
${R}_{y}=\sqrt{\frac{{I}_{y}}{M}},$
where ${I}_{y}$ is the moment of inertia about the $y$-axis.

- The radius of gyration ${R}_{0}$ about the origin is given by
${R}_{0}=\sqrt{\frac{{I}_{0}}{M}},$
where ${I}_{0}$ is the moment of inertia about the origin.

In polar coordinates, the region occupied by the plate is given by

$$
D=\{(r,\theta )\,:\,1\le r\le 2,\,\,0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{2}\}.
$$

The moment of inertia about the $y$-axis, in polar coordinates, is defined as

$$
{I}_{y}={∬}_{D}\lambda (r,\theta ){r}^{3}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta ,
$$

where $\lambda (r,\theta )$ is the mass density function.

Also, the mass density in terms of polar coordinates is $\lambda (r,\theta )=\frac{3}{7}Mr\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .$
Therefore, the moment of inertia about the $y$-axis is

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}_{y} & ={∬}_{D}\lambda (r,\theta ){r}^{3}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{3}{7}M{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{1}^{2}{r}^{4}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{3}{7}M({\int }_{1}^{2}{r}^{4}\,\text{d}r)({\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta ) \\  & =\frac{3}{7}M\cdot \frac{1}{5}{r}^{5}{|}_{1}^{2}\cdot {[-\frac{{cos}^{3}⁡\theta }{3}]}_{0}^{\pi /2} \\  & =\frac{3}{7}M\cdot (\frac{32}{5}-\frac{1}{5})\cdot (-0+\frac{1}{3}) \\  & =\frac{3}{7}M\cdot \frac{31}{5}\cdot \frac{1}{3} \\  & =\frac{31M}{35}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the radius of gyration about the $x$-axis is

$$
\begin{aligned}{R}_{y} & =\sqrt{\frac{{I}_{y}}{M}} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{31M}{35}\cdot \frac{1}{M}} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{31}{35}}.\end{aligned}

Question 5
?

A plate of mass M occupies the region D in the first quadrant bounded by the circles x2+y2=1, x2+y2=4, and the coordinate axes, as shown above. Its mass density at any point is given by λ(x,y)=37My. Find the radius of gyration of the plate about the y-axis.

a
 3135
b
 1115
c
 56
d
 1721
e
 710
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

For a plane lamina in the shape of a region D with mass M and mass density function λ(x,y), we have the following definitions:

  • The radius of gyration Rx about the x-axis is given by Rx=IxM, where Ix is the moment of inertia about the x-axis.

  • The radius of gyration Ry about the y-axis is given by Ry=IyM, where Iy is the moment of inertia about the y-axis.

  • The radius of gyration R0 about the origin is given by R0=I0M, where I0 is the moment of inertia about the origin.

In polar coordinates, the region occupied by the plate is given by D={(r,θ):1≤r≤2,0≤θ≤π2}.

The moment of inertia about the y-axis, in polar coordinates, is defined as

Iy=∬Dλ(r,θ)r3cos2⁡θdrdθ,

where λ(r,θ) is the mass density function.

Also, the mass density in terms of polar coordinates is λ(r,θ)=37Mrsin⁡θ. Therefore, the moment of inertia about the y-axis is

Iy=∬Dλ(r,θ)r3cos2⁡θdrdθ=37M∫0π/2∫12r4cos2⁡θsin⁡θdrdθ=37M(∫12r4dr)(∫0π/2cos2⁡θsin⁡θdθ)=37M⋅15r5|12⋅[−cos3⁡θ3]0π/2=37M⋅(325−15)⋅(−0+13)=37M⋅315⋅13=31M35.

Therefore, the radius of gyration about the x-axis is

Ry=IyM=31M35⋅1M=3135.

For a plane lamina in the shape of a region $D$ with mass $M$ and mass density function $\lambda (x,y),$ we have the following definitions:

- The radius of gyration ${R}_{x}$ about the $x$-axis is given by
${R}_{x}=\sqrt{\frac{{I}_{x}}{M}},$
where ${I}_{x}$ is the moment of inertia about the $x$-axis.

- The radius of gyration ${R}_{y}$ about the $y$-axis is given by
${R}_{y}=\sqrt{\frac{{I}_{y}}{M}},$
where ${I}_{y}$ is the moment of inertia about the $y$-axis.

- The radius of gyration ${R}_{0}$ about the origin is given by
${R}_{0}=\sqrt{\frac{{I}_{0}}{M}},$
where ${I}_{0}$ is the moment of inertia about the origin.

In polar coordinates, the region occupied by the plate is given by

$$
D=\{(r,\theta )\,:\,1\le r\le 2,\,\,0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{2}\}.
$$

The moment of inertia about the $y$-axis, in polar coordinates, is defined as

$$
{I}_{y}={∬}_{D}\lambda (r,\theta ){r}^{3}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta ,
$$

where $\lambda (r,\theta )$ is the mass density function.

Also, the mass density in terms of polar coordinates is $\lambda (r,\theta )=\frac{3}{7}Mr\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .$
Therefore, the moment of inertia about the $y$-axis is

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}_{y} & ={∬}_{D}\lambda (r,\theta ){r}^{3}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{3}{7}M{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{1}^{2}{r}^{4}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{3}{7}M({\int }_{1}^{2}{r}^{4}\,\text{d}r)({\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta ) \\  & =\frac{3}{7}M\cdot \frac{1}{5}{r}^{5}{|}_{1}^{2}\cdot {[-\frac{{cos}^{3}⁡\theta }{3}]}_{0}^{\pi /2} \\  & =\frac{3}{7}M\cdot (\frac{32}{5}-\frac{1}{5})\cdot (-0+\frac{1}{3}) \\  & =\frac{3}{7}M\cdot \frac{31}{5}\cdot \frac{1}{3} \\  & =\frac{31M}{35}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the radius of gyration about the $x$-axis is

$$
\begin{aligned}{R}_{y} & =\sqrt{\frac{{I}_{y}}{M}} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{31M}{35}\cdot \frac{1}{M}} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{31}{35}}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 5
?

A plate of mass M occupies the region D in the first quadrant bounded by the circles x2+y2=1, x2+y2=4, and the coordinate axes, as shown above. Its mass density at any point is given by λ(x,y)=37My. Find the radius of gyration of the plate about the y-axis.

a
 3135
b
 1115
c
 56
d
 1721
e
 710
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

For a plane lamina in the shape of a region D with mass M and mass density function λ(x,y), we have the following definitions:

  • The radius of gyration Rx about the x-axis is given by Rx=IxM, where Ix is the moment of inertia about the x-axis.

  • The radius of gyration Ry about the y-axis is given by Ry=IyM, where Iy is the moment of inertia about the y-axis.

  • The radius of gyration R0 about the origin is given by R0=I0M, where I0 is the moment of inertia about the origin.

In polar coordinates, the region occupied by the plate is given by D={(r,θ):1≤r≤2,0≤θ≤π2}.

The moment of inertia about the y-axis, in polar coordinates, is defined as

Iy=∬Dλ(r,θ)r3cos2⁡θdrdθ,

where λ(r,θ) is the mass density function.

Also, the mass density in terms of polar coordinates is λ(r,θ)=37Mrsin⁡θ. Therefore, the moment of inertia about the y-axis is

Iy=∬Dλ(r,θ)r3cos2⁡θdrdθ=37M∫0π/2∫12r4cos2⁡θsin⁡θdrdθ=37M(∫12r4dr)(∫0π/2cos2⁡θsin⁡θdθ)=37M⋅15r5|12⋅[−cos3⁡θ3]0π/2=37M⋅(325−15)⋅(−0+13)=37M⋅315⋅13=31M35.

Therefore, the radius of gyration about the x-axis is

Ry=IyM=31M35⋅1M=3135.

solution.reasoning: In polar coordinates, 1≤r≤2 and 0≤θ≤π/2, with density (3M/7)r sinθ. The total mass is (3M/7)(∫₁²r² dr)(∫₀^{π/2}sinθ dθ)=M. About the y-axis, I_y=∫∫x²λ dA=(3M/7)(∫₁²r⁴ dr)(∫₀^{π/2}cos²θ sinθ dθ)=(3M/7)(31/5)(1/3)=31M/35. Thus the radius of gyration is √(I_y/M)=√(31/35), option a. feedback.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14151907/assets/5b8ddb36e814517af21d790374e1fb192141bd6ef0fd99e83a147c6ed5a62aea.png)

A plate of mass $M$ occupies the region $D$ in the first quadrant bounded by the circles ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=1,$ ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=4,$ and the coordinate axes, as shown above. Its mass density at any point is given by $\lambda (x,y)=\frac{3}{7}My.$ Find the radius of gyration of the plate about the $y$-axis.
feedback.worked_solution:
For a plane lamina in the shape of a region $D$ with mass $M$ and mass density function $\lambda (x,y),$ we have the following definitions:

- The radius of gyration ${R}_{x}$ about the $x$-axis is given by
${R}_{x}=\sqrt{\frac{{I}_{x}}{M}},$
where ${I}_{x}$ is the moment of inertia about the $x$-axis.

- The radius of gyration ${R}_{y}$ about the $y$-axis is given by
${R}_{y}=\sqrt{\frac{{I}_{y}}{M}},$
where ${I}_{y}$ is the moment of inertia about the $y$-axis.

- The radius of gyration ${R}_{0}$ about the origin is given by
${R}_{0}=\sqrt{\frac{{I}_{0}}{M}},$
where ${I}_{0}$ is the moment of inertia about the origin.

In polar coordinates, the region occupied by the plate is given by

$$
D=\{(r,\theta )\,:\,1\le r\le 2,\,\,0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{2}\}.
$$

The moment of inertia about the $y$-axis, in polar coordinates, is defined as

$$
{I}_{y}={∬}_{D}\lambda (r,\theta ){r}^{3}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta ,
$$

where $\lambda (r,\theta )$ is the mass density function.

Also, the mass density in terms of polar coordinates is $\lambda (r,\theta )=\frac{3}{7}Mr\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .$
Therefore, the moment of inertia about the $y$-axis is

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}_{y} & ={∬}_{D}\lambda (r,\theta ){r}^{3}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{3}{7}M{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{1}^{2}{r}^{4}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{3}{7}M({\int }_{1}^{2}{r}^{4}\,\text{d}r)({\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta ) \\  & =\frac{3}{7}M\cdot \frac{1}{5}{r}^{5}{|}_{1}^{2}\cdot {[-\frac{{cos}^{3}⁡\theta }{3}]}_{0}^{\pi /2} \\  & =\frac{3}{7}M\cdot (\frac{32}{5}-\frac{1}{5})\cdot (-0+\frac{1}{3}) \\  & =\frac{3}{7}M\cdot \frac{31}{5}\cdot \frac{1}{3} \\  & =\frac{31M}{35}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the radius of gyration about the $x$-axis is

$$
\begin{aligned}{R}_{y} & =\sqrt{\frac{{I}_{y}}{M}} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{31M}{35}\cdot \frac{1}{M}} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{31}{35}}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 1
questions.problem:
The continuous random variable $X$ has the following probability density function:

$$
f(x)=\frac{1}{2x},\,{e}^{-2}<x<1
$$

Given that $\text{E}[X]=\frac{1}{2}-\frac{1}{2{e}^{2}},$ compute $\text{E}[4{X}^{2}-2X].$

*Hint: You may assume that $\text{E}[aX+bY]=a\text{E}[X]+b\text{E}[Y]$ for any random variables $X$ and $Y$ and constants $a$ and $b.$*
questions.worked_solution:
First, we simplify using the hint and the properties of expected value:

$$
\text{E}[4{X}^{2}-2X]=4\text{E}[{X}^{2}]-2\text{E}[X]
$$

For a continuous random variable $X$ with probability density function $f(x)$ defined over a set $S,$ the $n$th raw moment of $X$ is given by

$$
\text{E}[{X}^{n}]={\int }_{S}{x}^{n}\cdot f(x)\,\text{d}x.
$$

We already know $\text{E}[X].$ So, we compute the second raw moment of $X$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[{X}^{2}] & ={\int }_{S}{x}^{2}\cdot f(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{{e}^{-2}}^{1}{x}^{2}\cdot \frac{1}{2x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{{e}^{-2}}^{1}\frac{x}{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\frac{{x}^{2}}{4}\,|}_{{e}^{-2}}^{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}-\frac{1}{4{e}^{4}}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $\text{E}[X]=\frac{1}{2}-\frac{1}{2{e}^{2}}$ and $\text{E}[{X}^{2}]=\frac{1}{4}-\frac{1}{4{e}^{4}}$ into the simplified expression, we conclude that

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[4{X}^{2}-2X] & =4\text{E}[{X}^{2}]-2\text{E}[X] \\  & =4(\frac{1}{4}-\frac{1}{4{e}^{4}})-2(\frac{1}{2}-\frac{1}{2{e}^{2}}) \\  & =1-\frac{1}{{e}^{4}}-1+\frac{1}{{e}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{1}{{e}^{2}}-\frac{1}{{e}^{4}}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 2
questions.problem:
Given that $X$ is a continuous random variable with the following probability density function, compute $\text{E}[10-4{X}^{2}].$

$$
f(x)=\frac{2}{{x}^{2}},\,1<x<2
$$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we simplify using the properties of expected value:

$$
\text{E}[10-4{X}^{2}]=10-4\text{E}[{X}^{2}]
$$

For a continuous random variable $X$ with probability density function $f(x)$ defined over a set $S,$ the $n$th raw moment of $X$ is given by

$$
\text{E}[{X}^{n}]={\int }_{S}{x}^{n}\cdot f(x)\,\text{d}x.
$$

So, we compute the second raw moment of $X$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[{X}^{2}] & ={\int }_{S}{x}^{2}\cdot f(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}{x}^{2}\cdot \frac{2}{{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}2\,\text{d}x \\  & =2x\,{|}_{1}^{2} \\  & =2\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $\text{E}[{X}^{2}]=2$ into the simplified expression, we conclude that

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[10-4{X}^{2}] & =10-4\text{E}[{X}^{2}] \\  & =10-4\cdot 2 \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 3
questions.problem:
The continuous random variable $X$ has the following probability density function:

$$
f(x)=\frac{3{x}^{2}+4}{5},\,0<x<1
$$

Given that $\text{E}[X]=\frac{11}{20},$ compute $\text{E}[2X-{X}^{3}+1].$

*Hint: You may assume that $\text{E}[aX+bY]=a\text{E}[X]+b\text{E}[Y]$ for any random variables $X$ and $Y$ and constants $a$ and $b.$*
questions.worked_solution:
First, we simplify using the hint and the properties of expected value:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[2X-{X}^{3}+1] & =2\text{E}[X]-\text{E}[{X}^{3}]+\text{E}[1] \\  & =2\text{E}[X]-\text{E}[{X}^{3}]+1\end{aligned}
$$

For a continuous random variable $X$ with probability density function $f(x)$ defined over a set $S,$ the $n$th raw moment of $X$ is given by

$$
\text{E}[{X}^{n}]={\int }_{S}{x}^{n}\cdot f(x)\,\text{d}x.
$$

We already know $\text{E}[X].$ So, we compute the third raw moment of $X$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[{X}^{3}] & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{x}^{3}\cdot (\frac{3{x}^{2}+4}{5})\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(\frac{3}{5}{x}^{5}+\frac{4}{5}{x}^{3})\text{d}x \\  & ={(\frac{1}{10}{x}^{6}+\frac{1}{5}{x}^{4})|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{10}+\frac{1}{5} \\  & =\frac{3}{10}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $\text{E}[X]=\frac{11}{20}$ and $\text{E}[{X}^{3}]=\frac{3}{10}$ into the simplified expression, we conclude that

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[2X-{X}^{3}+1] & =2\text{E}[X]-\text{E}[{X}^{3}]+1 \\  & =2\cdot \frac{11}{20}-\frac{3}{10}+1 \\  & =\frac{11}{10}-\frac{3}{10}+1 \\  & =\frac{9}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 4
questions.problem:
A continuous random variable $X$ has the probability density function 

$$
f(x)=\frac{1}{4}(1-x),\,-2\le x\le 0.
$$

Calculate $\text{E}[{X}^{3}].$
questions.worked_solution:
For a continuous random variable $X$ with probability density function $f(x)$ defined over a set $S,$ the $n$th raw moment of $X$ is given by

$$
\text{E}[{X}^{n}]={\int }_{S}{x}^{n}\cdot f(x)\,\text{d}x.
$$

So, we compute the third raw moment of $X$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[{X}^{3}] & ={\int }_{-2}^{0}{x}^{3}\cdot \frac{1}{4}(1-x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{4}{\int }_{-2}^{0}({x}^{3}-{x}^{4})\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{4}(\frac{1}{4}{x}^{4}-\frac{1}{5}{x}^{5}){|}_{-2}^{0} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}(0-[4+\frac{32}{5}]) \\  & =\frac{1}{4}(-\frac{52}{5}) \\  & =-\frac{13}{5}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 5
questions.problem:
A continuous random variable $X$ has the probability density function 

$$
f(x)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{4}, & 0\le x<1 \\ \frac{1}{{x}^{5}}, & x\ge 1.\end{aligned}
$$

Calculate $\text{E}[{X}^{3}].$
questions.worked_solution:
For a continuous random variable $X$ with probability density function $f(x)$ defined over a set $S,$ the $n$th raw moment of $X$ is given by

$$
\text{E}[{X}^{n}]={\int }_{S}{x}^{n}\cdot f(x)\,\text{d}x.
$$

So, we compute the third raw moment of $X$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[{X}^{3}] & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{x}^{3}\cdot f(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{x}^{3}\cdot \frac{3}{4}\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{1}^{\infty }{x}^{3}\cdot \frac{1}{{x}^{5}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{3}{4}{\int }_{0}^{1}{x}^{3}\,\text{d}x+{lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{1}^{a}\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{3}{16}\,{x}^{4}\,{|}_{0}^{1}+{lim}_{a\to \infty }(-\frac{1}{x}){|}_{1}^{a} \\  & =\frac{3}{16}(1-0)+{lim}_{a\to \infty }(1-\frac{1}{a}) \\  & =\frac{3}{16}+(1-0) \\  & =\frac{19}{16}\end{aligned}
$$

observed_steps.name: Question 1
observed_steps.worked_solution:
First, we simplify using the hint and the properties of expected value:

$$
\text{E}[4{X}^{2}-2X]=4\text{E}[{X}^{2}]-2\text{E}[X]
$$

For a continuous random variable $X$ with probability density function $f(x)$ defined over a set $S,$ the $n$th raw moment of $X$ is given by

$$
\text{E}[{X}^{n}]={\int }_{S}{x}^{n}\cdot f(x)\,\text{d}x.
$$

We already know $\text{E}[X].$ So, we compute the second raw moment of $X$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[{X}^{2}] & ={\int }_{S}{x}^{2}\cdot f(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{{e}^{-2}}^{1}{x}^{2}\cdot \frac{1}{2x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{{e}^{-2}}^{1}\frac{x}{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\frac{{x}^{2}}{4}\,|}_{{e}^{-2}}^{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}-\frac{1}{4{e}^{4}}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $\text{E}[X]=\frac{1}{2}-\frac{1}{2{e}^{2}}$ and $\text{E}[{X}^{2}]=\frac{1}{4}-\frac{1}{4{e}^{4}}$ into the simplified expression, we conclude that

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[4{X}^{2}-2X] & =4\text{E}[{X}^{2}]-2\text{E}[X] \\  & =4(\frac{1}{4}-\frac{1}{4{e}^{4}})-2(\frac{1}{2}-\frac{1}{2{e}^{2}}) \\  & =1-\frac{1}{{e}^{4}}-1+\frac{1}{{e}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{1}{{e}^{2}}-\frac{1}{{e}^{4}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 1
?

The continuous random variable X has the following probability density function: f(x)=12x,e−2<x<1 Given that E[X]=12−12e2, compute E[4X2−2X].

Hint: You may assume that E[aX+bY]=aE[X]+bE[Y] for any random variables X and Y and constants a and b.

a
1e−1
b
1e
c
1e2−1e4
d
1e2+2
e
1−1e
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we simplify using the hint and the properties of expected value: E[4X2−2X]=4E[X2]−2E[X]

For a continuous random variable X with probability density function f(x) defined over a set S, the nth raw moment of X is given by E[Xn]=∫Sxn⋅f(x)dx.

We already know E[X]. So, we compute the second raw moment of X as follows: E[X2]=∫Sx2⋅f(x)dx=∫e−21x2⋅12xdx=∫e−21x2dx=x24|e−21=14−14e4

Substituting E[X]=12−12e2 and E[X2]=14−14e4 into the simplified expression, we conclude that E[4X2−2X]=4E[X2]−2E[X]=4(14−14e4)−2(12−12e2)=1−1e4−1+1e2=1e2−1e4.

observed_steps.name: Question 2
observed_steps.worked_solution:
First, we simplify using the properties of expected value:

$$
\text{E}[10-4{X}^{2}]=10-4\text{E}[{X}^{2}]
$$

For a continuous random variable $X$ with probability density function $f(x)$ defined over a set $S,$ the $n$th raw moment of $X$ is given by

$$
\text{E}[{X}^{n}]={\int }_{S}{x}^{n}\cdot f(x)\,\text{d}x.
$$

So, we compute the second raw moment of $X$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[{X}^{2}] & ={\int }_{S}{x}^{2}\cdot f(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}{x}^{2}\cdot \frac{2}{{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}2\,\text{d}x \\  & =2x\,{|}_{1}^{2} \\  & =2\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $\text{E}[{X}^{2}]=2$ into the simplified expression, we conclude that

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[10-4{X}^{2}] & =10-4\text{E}[{X}^{2}] \\  & =10-4\cdot 2 \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

observed_steps.name: Question 3
observed_steps.worked_solution:
First, we simplify using the hint and the properties of expected value:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[2X-{X}^{3}+1] & =2\text{E}[X]-\text{E}[{X}^{3}]+\text{E}[1] \\  & =2\text{E}[X]-\text{E}[{X}^{3}]+1\end{aligned}
$$

For a continuous random variable $X$ with probability density function $f(x)$ defined over a set $S,$ the $n$th raw moment of $X$ is given by

$$
\text{E}[{X}^{n}]={\int }_{S}{x}^{n}\cdot f(x)\,\text{d}x.
$$

We already know $\text{E}[X].$ So, we compute the third raw moment of $X$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[{X}^{3}] & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{x}^{3}\cdot (\frac{3{x}^{2}+4}{5})\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(\frac{3}{5}{x}^{5}+\frac{4}{5}{x}^{3})\text{d}x \\  & ={(\frac{1}{10}{x}^{6}+\frac{1}{5}{x}^{4})|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{10}+\frac{1}{5} \\  & =\frac{3}{10}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $\text{E}[X]=\frac{11}{20}$ and $\text{E}[{X}^{3}]=\frac{3}{10}$ into the simplified expression, we conclude that

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[2X-{X}^{3}+1] & =2\text{E}[X]-\text{E}[{X}^{3}]+1 \\  & =2\cdot \frac{11}{20}-\frac{3}{10}+1 \\  & =\frac{11}{10}-\frac{3}{10}+1 \\  & =\frac{9}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

a
95

Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we simplify using the hint and the properties of expected value:

E[2X−X3+1]=2E[X]−E[X3]+E[1]=2E[X]−E[X3]+1

For a continuous random variable X with probability density function f(x) defined over a set S, the nth raw moment of X is given by

E[Xn]=∫Sxn⋅f(x)dx.

We already know E[X]. So, we compute the third raw moment of X as follows: E[X3]=∫01x3⋅(3x2+45)dx=∫01(35x5+45x3)dx=(110x6+15x4)|01=110+15=310

E[2X−X3+1]=2E[X]−E[X3]+1=2⋅1120−310+1=1110−310+1=95.

For a continuous random variable $X$ with probability density function $f(x)$ defined over a set $S,$ the $n$th raw moment of $X$ is given by

$$
\text{E}[{X}^{n}]={\int }_{S}{x}^{n}\cdot f(x)\,\text{d}x.
$$

So, we compute the third raw moment of $X$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[{X}^{3}] & ={\int }_{-2}^{0}{x}^{3}\cdot \frac{1}{4}(1-x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{4}{\int }_{-2}^{0}({x}^{3}-{x}^{4})\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{4}(\frac{1}{4}{x}^{4}-\frac{1}{5}{x}^{5}){|}_{-2}^{0} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}(0-[4+\frac{32}{5}]) \\  & =\frac{1}{4}(-\frac{52}{5}) \\  & =-\frac{13}{5}\end{aligned}
$$
