questions.name: Question 7
questions.problem: Given that $h(r,\theta )=r(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -1),$ find $\frac{∂h}{∂x},$ where $(x,y)$ are Cartesian coordinates and $(r,\theta )$ are the corresponding plane polar coordinates.
questions.worked_solution:
We will make use of the following chain rule formula:

$$
\frac{∂h}{∂x}=\frac{∂h}{∂r}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -\frac{1}{r}\frac{∂h}{∂\theta }\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $h$ with respect to $r$ and $\theta :$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂h}{∂r}=\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -1,\,\frac{∂h}{∂\theta }=-r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \end{aligned}
$$

Then, substituting these into our chain rule formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂h}{∂x} & =(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -1)\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -\frac{1}{r}(-r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & ={cos}^{2}⁡\theta -\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta  \\  & =1-\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 8
questions.problem: Given that $v(r,\theta )=r(1+\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta ),$ find $\frac{∂v}{∂y},$ where $(x,y)$ are Cartesian coordinates and $(r,\theta )$ are the corresponding plane polar coordinates.
questions.worked_solution:
We will make use of the following chain rule formula:

$$
\frac{∂v}{∂y}=\frac{∂v}{∂r}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +\frac{1}{r}\frac{∂v}{∂\theta }\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $v$ with respect to $r$ and $\theta :$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂v}{∂r}=1+\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta ,\,\frac{∂v}{∂\theta }=-2r\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta \end{aligned}
$$

Then, substituting these into our chain rule formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂v}{∂y} & =(1+\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta )\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +\frac{1}{r}(-2r\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta )\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta -2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 9
questions.problem: Given that $v(r,\theta )=r(2+\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ),$ find $\frac{∂v}{∂x},$ where $(x,y)$ are Cartesian coordinates and $(r,\theta )$ are the corresponding plane polar coordinates.
questions.worked_solution:
We will make use of the following chain rule formula:

$$
\frac{∂v}{∂x}=\frac{∂v}{∂r}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -\frac{1}{r}\frac{∂v}{∂\theta }\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta 
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $v$ with respect to $r$ and $\theta :$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂v}{∂r}=2+\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,\frac{∂v}{∂\theta }=-r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \end{aligned}
$$

Then, substituting these into our chain rule formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂v}{∂x} & =(2+\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -\frac{1}{r}(-r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta  \\  & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +1.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 10
questions.problem: Given that $v(r,\theta )={r}^{2}+2r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,$ find $\frac{∂v}{∂x},$ where $(x,y)$ are Cartesian coordinates and $(r,\theta )$ are the corresponding plane polar coordinates.
questions.worked_solution:
We will make use of the following chain rule formula:

$$
\frac{∂v}{∂x}=\frac{∂v}{∂r}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -\frac{1}{r}\frac{∂v}{∂\theta }\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta 
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $v$ with respect to $r$ and $\theta :$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂v}{∂r}=2r+2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,\frac{∂v}{∂\theta }=-2r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \end{aligned}
$$

Then, substituting these into our chain rule formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂v}{∂x} & =(2r+2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -\frac{1}{r}(-2r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =2r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +2{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +2{sin}^{2}⁡\theta  \\  & =2r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +2({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta ) \\  & =2r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +2.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 11
questions.problem: Given that $g(x,y,z)={x}^{2}z+{z}^{2},$ find $\frac{∂g}{∂z},$ where $(x,y,z)$ are Cartesian coordinates and $(r,\theta ,z)$ are the corresponding cylindrical polar coordinates.
questions.worked_solution:
Applying the multivariable chain rule for the function $g(x,y,z)$ with three independent variables $r,\theta ,$ and $z,$ where $x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,$ and $z=z,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂g}{∂z} & =\frac{∂g}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂z}+\frac{∂g}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂z}+\frac{∂g}{∂z}\cdot \frac{∂z}{∂z} \\  & =\frac{∂g}{∂z}.\end{aligned}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $g$ with respect to $z:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂g}{∂z}={x}^{2}+2z\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $r,\theta ,$ and $z,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂g}{∂z} & ={r}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +2z.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 12
questions.problem: Given that $w(x,y,z)=x{z}^{4}+y,$ find $\frac{∂w}{∂r},$ where $(x,y,z)$ are Cartesian coordinates and $(r,\theta ,z)$ are the corresponding cylindrical polar coordinates.
questions.worked_solution:
Applying the multivariable chain rule for the function $w(x,y,z)$ with three independent variables $r,\theta ,$ and $z,$ where $x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,$ and $z=z,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂w}{∂r} & =\frac{∂w}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂r}+\frac{∂w}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂r}+\frac{∂w}{∂z}\cdot \frac{∂z}{∂r} \\  & =\frac{∂w}{∂x}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\frac{∂w}{∂y}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $w$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂w}{∂x}={z}^{4},\,\frac{∂w}{∂y}=1\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $r,\theta ,$ and $z,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂w}{∂x} & ={z}^{4}, \\ \frac{∂w}{∂y} & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting these into our chain rule formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂w}{∂r} & =({z}^{4})\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +(1)\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & ={z}^{4}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 13
questions.problem: Given that $h(x,y,z)=xyz,$ find $\frac{∂h}{∂\theta },$ where $(x,y,z)$ are Cartesian coordinates and $(r,\theta ,z)$ are the corresponding cylindrical polar coordinates.
questions.worked_solution:
Applying the multivariable chain rule for the function $h(x,y,z)$ with three independent variables $r,\theta ,$ and $z,$ where $x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,$ and $z=z,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂h}{∂\theta } & =\frac{∂h}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂\theta }+\frac{∂h}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂\theta }+\frac{∂h}{∂z}\cdot \frac{∂z}{∂\theta } \\  & =-\frac{∂h}{∂x}r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +\frac{∂h}{∂y}r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $h$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂h}{∂x}=yz,\,\frac{∂h}{∂y}=xz\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $r,\theta ,$ and $z,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂h}{∂x} & =rz\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta , \\ \frac{∂h}{∂y} & =rz\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting these into our chain rule formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂h}{∂\theta } & =-(rz\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +(rz\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =-{r}^{2}z{sin}^{2}⁡\theta +{r}^{2}z{cos}^{2}⁡\theta  \\  & ={r}^{2}z({cos}^{2}⁡\theta -{sin}^{2}⁡\theta ) \\  & ={r}^{2}z\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 14
questions.problem: Given that $f(x,y,z)={x}^{2}+{y}^{3}+{z}^{4},$ find $\frac{∂f}{∂r},$ where $(x,y,z)$ are Cartesian coordinates and $(r,\theta ,z)$ are the corresponding cylindrical polar coordinates.
questions.worked_solution:
Applying the multivariable chain rule for the function $f(x,y,z)$ with three independent variables $r,\theta ,$ and $z,$ where $x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,$ and $z=z,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂r} & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂r}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂r}+\frac{∂f}{∂z}\cdot \frac{∂z}{∂r} \\  & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\frac{∂f}{∂y}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=2x,\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=3{y}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $r,\theta ,$ and $z,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =2r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta , \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =3{r}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting these into our chain rule formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂r} & =(2r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +(3{r}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =2r{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +3{r}^{2}{sin}^{3}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 15
questions.problem: Given that $f(x,y,z)=xy{z}^{2},$ find $\frac{∂f}{∂z},$ where $(x,y,z)$ are Cartesian coordinates and $(r,\theta ,z)$ are the corresponding cylindrical polar coordinates.
questions.worked_solution:
Applying the multivariable chain rule for the function $f(x,y,z)$ with three independent variables $r,\theta ,$ and $z,$ where $x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,$ and $z=z,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂z} & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂z}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂z}+\frac{∂f}{∂z}\cdot \frac{∂z}{∂z} \\  & =\frac{∂f}{∂z}.\end{aligned}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $z:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂z}=2xyz\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $r,\theta ,$ and $z,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂z} & =2{r}^{2}z\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & ={r}^{2}z\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta ).\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Calculating the Derivative of a Cartesian Function With Respect to Plane Polar Coordinates
canonical_examples.problem: Given that $f(x,y)=\dfrac12x^2+y^2,$ find $\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial \theta},$ where $(x,y)$ are Cartesian coordinates and $(r,\theta)$ are the corresponding plane polar coordinates.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Applying the multivariable chain rule for the function $f(x,y)$ with two independent variables $r$ and $\theta,$ where $x=r\cos\theta$ and $y=r\sin\theta,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂\theta } & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂\theta }+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂\theta } \\  & =-\frac{∂f}{∂x}r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +\frac{∂f}{∂y}r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=x,\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=2y\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $r$ and $\theta,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta , \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =2r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting these into our chain rule formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂\theta } & =-(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +(2r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =-{r}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +2{r}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & ={r}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{r}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta ).\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.problem: Given that $w(r, \theta)=r \cos 3\theta,$ find $\dfrac{\partial w}{\partial x},$ where $(x,y)$ are Cartesian coordinates and $(r,\theta)$ are the corresponding plane polar coordinates.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
We will make use of the following chain rule formula:

$$
\dfrac{\partial w}{\partial x} = \dfrac{\partial w}{\partial r}\cos\theta - \dfrac{1}{r}\dfrac{\partial w}{\partial \theta}\sin\theta
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $w$ with respect to $r$ and $\theta{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂w}{∂r}=\operatorname{cos}⁡3\theta ,\,\frac{∂w}{∂\theta }=-3r\operatorname{sin}⁡3\theta \end{aligned}
$$

Then, substituting these into our chain rule formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂w}{∂x} & =(\operatorname{cos}⁡3\theta )\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -\frac{1}{r}(-3r\operatorname{sin}⁡3\theta )\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡3\theta +3\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡3\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.problem: Given that $w(x,y,z)=z^3(x^2+2y^2),$ find $\dfrac{\partial w}{\partial \theta},$ where $(x,y,z)$ are Cartesian coordinates and $(r,\theta,z)$ are the corresponding cylindrical polar coordinates.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Applying the multivariable chain rule for the function $w(x,y,z)$ with three independent variables $r, \theta,$ and $z,$ where $x=r\cos\theta, y=r\sin\theta,$ and $z=z,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂w}{∂\theta } & =\frac{∂w}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂\theta }+\frac{∂w}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂\theta }+\frac{∂w}{∂z}\cdot \frac{∂z}{∂\theta } \\  & =-\frac{∂w}{∂x}r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +\frac{∂w}{∂y}r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $w$ with respect to $x$ and $y{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂w}{∂x}=2x{z}^{3},\,\frac{∂w}{∂y}=4y{z}^{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $r, \theta,$ and $z,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂w}{∂x} & =2r{z}^{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta , \\ \frac{∂w}{∂y} & =4r{z}^{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting these into our chain rule formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂w}{∂\theta } & =-(2r{z}^{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +(4r{z}^{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =-2{r}^{2}{z}^{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +4{r}^{2}{z}^{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =2{r}^{2}{z}^{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & ={r}^{2}{z}^{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Given a function $f(x,y),$ how do we calculate the partial derivatives $f_r$ and $f_\theta,$ where $(r,\theta)$ are plane polar coordinates?

To do this, we can use the multivariable chain rule. First, let's write down our tree diagram.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14156360/assets/7f19c4a682b30f1eea1d9c1be7da83bd77ba137173f25eb9c7e5cf253abba015.png)

From the tree diagram, we can see that

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂r} & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂r}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂r} \\ \frac{∂f}{∂\theta } & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂\theta }+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂\theta }.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's take the partial derivatives of $x=r\cos\theta$ and $y=r\sin\theta$ with respect to $r$ and $\theta{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂r} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  &  &  & \frac{∂y}{∂r} & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ \frac{∂x}{∂\theta } & =-r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  &  &  & \frac{∂y}{∂\theta } & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \end{aligned}
$$

Substituting these results into the multivariable chain rule, we conclude that

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂r} & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\frac{∂f}{∂y}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta , \\ \frac{∂f}{∂\theta } & =-\frac{∂f}{∂x}r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +\frac{∂f}{∂y}r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

tutorials.problem:
Up to now, we've been using the following formulas:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{r} & ={f}_{x}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +{f}_{y}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ {f}_{\theta } & =-r{f}_{x}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +r{f}_{y}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \end{aligned}
$$

We can treat the above as a system of equations in the "unknowns" $f_x$ and $f_y.$ Solving this system gives explicit expressions for $f_x$ and $f_y$ in terms of functions of $r$ and $\theta.$

For example, suppose we want an explicit formula for $f_x.$ We can eliminate $f_y$ by multiplying the first equation by $r\cos\theta$ and the second equation by $\sin\theta$ to give

$$
\begin{aligned}r{f}_{r}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & =r{f}_{x}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +r{f}_{y}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta , \\ {f}_{\theta }\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & =-r{f}_{x}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta +r{f}_{y}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Subtracting the second equation from the first gives

$$
r f_r \cos\theta - f_\theta \sin\theta = r f_x(\sin^2\theta + \cos^2\theta),
$$

which simplifies to

$$
f_x = f_r \cos\theta - \dfrac1r f_\theta \sin\theta.
$$

We can use a similar procedure to write $f_y$ in terms of functions of $r$ and $\theta.$ Our results as summarized below:

$$
\eqalign{
\dfrac {\partial f}{\partial x} &= \dfrac {\partial f}{\partial r} \cos \theta
						-\dfrac{1}{r} \dfrac {\partial f}{\partial \theta}\sin \theta\[1ex]
\dfrac {\partial f}{\partial y} &= \dfrac {\partial f}{\partial r} \sin \theta
						+ \dfrac{1}{r} \dfrac {\partial f}{\partial \theta}\cos \theta
}
$$

tutorials.name: The Multivariable Chain Rule With Cylindrical Polar Coordinates
tutorials.problem:
Given a function of three variables $f(x,y,z),$ we can find formulas for $f_r, f_\theta,$ and $f_z,$ where $(r,\theta,z)$ are cylindrical polar coordinates. The results that we need are as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂r} & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\frac{∂f}{∂y}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ \frac{∂f}{∂\theta } & =-\frac{∂f}{∂x}r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +\frac{∂f}{∂y}r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ \frac{∂f}{∂z} & =\frac{∂f}{∂z}.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that the first and second equations are identical to the equations derived for plane polar coordinates, as we would expect. 

The difference here is that we now have a third equation that deals with the $z$-dependence. But since the $z$-coordinate is the same in both Cartesian and cylindrical polar coordinates, we can simply differentiate with respect to $z$ as usual.

Let's see an example.

tutorials.name: The Multivariable Chain Rule With Spherical Polar Coordinates
tutorials.problem:
Suppose that we have a function $f(x,y,z),$ and we wish to find formulas for $f_\rho,$ $f_\theta,$ and $f_\phi$, where $(\rho,\theta,\phi)$ are spherical polar coordinates.

Using the multivariable chain rule, it can be shown that

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂\rho } & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ+\frac{∂f}{∂z}\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂\theta } & =-\frac{∂f}{∂x}\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂ϕ} & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ-\frac{∂f}{∂z}\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ.\end{aligned}
$$

You might want to try deriving these formulas for yourself!

Question 1
?

Given that f(x,y)=2y−xy, find ∂f∂θ, where (x,y) are Cartesian coordinates and (r,θ) are the corresponding plane polar coordinates.

a
 2rsin⁡θ−rcos⁡θ
b
 r2(cos⁡θ+sin⁡(2θ))
c
2rcos⁡θ−r2cos⁡(2θ)
d
 r(sin⁡θ+cos⁡(2θ))
e
 cos⁡θ−r2sin⁡(2θ)
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Applying the multivariable chain rule for the function f(x,y) with two independent variables r and θ, where x=rcos⁡θ and y=rsin⁡θ, we have

∂f∂θ=∂f∂x⋅∂x∂θ+∂f∂y⋅∂y∂θ=−∂f∂xrsin⁡θ+∂f∂yrcos⁡θ.

First, we find the partial derivatives of f with respect to x and y: ∂f∂x=−y,∂f∂y=2−x

Writing the above results in terms of r and θ, we get

∂f∂x=−rsin⁡θ,∂f∂y=2−rcos⁡θ.

Finally, substituting these into our chain rule formula, we get ∂f∂θ=(−rsin⁡θ)(−rsin⁡θ)+(2−rcos⁡θ)rcos⁡θ=r2sin2⁡θ+2rcos⁡θ−r2cos2⁡θ=r2(sin2⁡θ−cos2⁡θ)+2rcos⁡θ=−r2cos⁡(2θ)+2rcos⁡θ=2rcos⁡θ−r2cos⁡(2θ).

Applying the multivariable chain rule for the function $g(x,y)$ with two independent variables $r$ and $\theta ,$ where $x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ and $y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂g}{∂r} & =\frac{∂g}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂r}+\frac{∂g}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂r} \\  & =\frac{∂g}{∂x}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\frac{∂g}{∂y}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $g$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂g}{∂x}=\frac{1}{x+y},\,\frac{∂g}{∂y}=\frac{1}{x+y}\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $r$ and $\theta ,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂g}{∂x} & =\frac{1}{r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }, \\ \frac{∂g}{∂y} & =\frac{1}{r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting these into our chain rule formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂g}{∂r} & =(\frac{1}{r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta })\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +(\frac{1}{r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta })\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }{r(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )} \\  & =\frac{1}{r}.\end{aligned}
$$

Given that g(x,y)=ln⁡(x+y), find ∂g∂r, where (x,y) are Cartesian coordinates and (r,θ) are the corresponding plane polar coordinates.

a
r
b
r2sin⁡θ
c
cos⁡θ−sin⁡θcos⁡θ+sin⁡θ
d
1rcos⁡θ+rsin⁡θ
e

EXPLANATION

Applying the multivariable chain rule for the function g(x,y) with two independent variables r and θ, where x=rcos⁡θ and y=rsin⁡θ, we have

∂g∂r=∂g∂x⋅∂x∂r+∂g∂y⋅∂y∂r=∂g∂xcos⁡θ+∂g∂ysin⁡θ.

First, we find the partial derivatives of g with respect to x and y:

∂g∂x=1x+y,∂g∂y=1x+y

Writing the above results in terms of r and θ, we get

∂g∂x=1rcos⁡θ+rsin⁡θ,∂g∂y=1rcos⁡θ+rsin⁡θ.

Finally, substituting these into our chain rule formula, we get

∂g∂r=(1rcos⁡θ+rsin⁡θ)cos⁡θ+(1rcos⁡θ+rsin⁡θ)sin⁡θ=cos⁡θ+sin⁡θr(cos⁡θ+sin⁡θ)=1r.

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂h}{∂r} & =\frac{∂h}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂r}+\frac{∂h}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂r} \\  & =\frac{∂h}{∂x}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\frac{∂h}{∂y}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $h$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂h}{∂x}=2x,\,\frac{∂h}{∂y}=-2y\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $r$ and $\theta ,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂h}{∂x} & =2r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta , \\ \frac{∂h}{∂y} & =-2r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting these into our chain rule formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂h}{∂r} & =(2r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -(2r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =2r({cos}^{2}⁡\theta -{sin}^{2}⁡\theta ) \\  & =2r\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta ).\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the multivariable chain rule for the function $f(x,y)$ with two independent variables $r$ and $\theta ,$ where $x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ and $y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂\theta } & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂\theta }+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂\theta } \\  & =-\frac{∂f}{∂x}r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +\frac{∂f}{∂y}r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=2x,\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=1\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $r$ and $\theta ,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =2r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta , \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting these into our chain rule formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂\theta } & =-2r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =-{r}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )+r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -{r}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta ).\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 5
?

Given that f(x,y)=x2+y, find ∂f∂θ, where (x,y) are Cartesian coordinates and (r,θ) are the corresponding plane polar coordinates.

a
 r(sin⁡(2θ)+rcos⁡(θ)
b
 rcos⁡θ+rsin⁡(2θ)
c
rcos⁡θ−r2sin⁡(2θ)
d
 r2(cos⁡θ−sin⁡θ)
e
 rsin⁡θ+r2sin⁡(2θ)
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Applying the multivariable chain rule for the function f(x,y) with two independent variables r and θ, where x=rcos⁡θ and y=rsin⁡θ, we have

∂f∂θ=∂f∂x⋅∂x∂θ+∂f∂y⋅∂y∂θ=−∂f∂xrsin⁡θ+∂f∂yrcos⁡θ.

First, we find the partial derivatives of f with respect to x and y: ∂f∂x=2x,∂f∂y=1

Writing the above results in terms of r and θ, we get

∂f∂x=2rcos⁡θ,∂f∂y=1.

Finally, substituting these into our chain rule formula, we get ∂f∂θ=−2rcos⁡θrsin⁡θ+rcos⁡θ=−r2sin⁡(2θ)+rcos⁡θ=rcos⁡θ−r2sin⁡(2θ).

tutorial.name: Differentiating of a Function Given in Polar Coordinates With Respect to Cartesian Coordinates
tutorial.problem:
Up to now, we've been using the following formulas:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{r} & ={f}_{x}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +{f}_{y}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ {f}_{\theta } & =-r{f}_{x}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +r{f}_{y}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \end{aligned}
$$

We can treat the above as a system of equations in the "unknowns" $f_x$ and $f_y.$ Solving this system gives explicit expressions for $f_x$ and $f_y$ in terms of functions of $r$ and $\theta.$

For example, suppose we want an explicit formula for $f_x.$ We can eliminate $f_y$ by multiplying the first equation by $r\cos\theta$ and the second equation by $\sin\theta$ to give

$$
\begin{aligned}r{f}_{r}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & =r{f}_{x}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +r{f}_{y}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta , \\ {f}_{\theta }\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & =-r{f}_{x}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta +r{f}_{y}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Subtracting the second equation from the first gives

$$
r f_r \cos\theta - f_\theta \sin\theta = r f_x(\sin^2\theta + \cos^2\theta),
$$

which simplifies to

$$
f_x = f_r \cos\theta - \dfrac1r f_\theta \sin\theta.
$$

We can use a similar procedure to write $f_y$ in terms of functions of $r$ and $\theta.$ Our results as summarized below:

$$
\eqalign{
\dfrac {\partial f}{\partial x} &= \dfrac {\partial f}{\partial r} \cos \theta
						-\dfrac{1}{r} \dfrac {\partial f}{\partial \theta}\sin \theta\[1ex]
\dfrac {\partial f}{\partial y} &= \dfrac {\partial f}{\partial r} \sin \theta
						+ \dfrac{1}{r} \dfrac {\partial f}{\partial \theta}\cos \theta
}
$$

$$
\dfrac{\partial w}{\partial x} = \dfrac{\partial w}{\partial r}\cos\theta - \dfrac{1}{r}\dfrac{\partial w}{\partial \theta}\sin\theta
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $w$ with respect to $r$ and $\theta{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂w}{∂r}=\operatorname{cos}⁡3\theta ,\,\frac{∂w}{∂\theta }=-3r\operatorname{sin}⁡3\theta \end{aligned}
$$

Then, substituting these into our chain rule formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂w}{∂x} & =(\operatorname{cos}⁡3\theta )\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -\frac{1}{r}(-3r\operatorname{sin}⁡3\theta )\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡3\theta +3\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡3\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

question.problem: Given that $w(r, \theta)=r \cos 3\theta,$ find $\dfrac{\partial w}{\partial x},$ where $(x,y)$ are Cartesian coordinates and $(r,\theta)$ are the corresponding plane polar coordinates.
question.worked_solution:
We will make use of the following chain rule formula:

$$
\dfrac{\partial w}{\partial x} = \dfrac{\partial w}{\partial r}\cos\theta - \dfrac{1}{r}\dfrac{\partial w}{\partial \theta}\sin\theta
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $w$ with respect to $r$ and $\theta{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂w}{∂r}=\operatorname{cos}⁡3\theta ,\,\frac{∂w}{∂\theta }=-3r\operatorname{sin}⁡3\theta \end{aligned}
$$

Then, substituting these into our chain rule formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂w}{∂x} & =(\operatorname{cos}⁡3\theta )\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -\frac{1}{r}(-3r\operatorname{sin}⁡3\theta )\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡3\theta +3\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡3\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

We will make use of the following chain rule formula:

$$
\frac{∂w}{∂y}=\frac{∂w}{∂r}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +\frac{1}{r}\frac{∂w}{∂\theta }\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta 
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $w$ with respect to $r$ and $\theta :$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂w}{∂r}=1+\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta ,\,\frac{∂w}{∂\theta }=2r\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta \end{aligned}
$$

Then, substituting these into our chain rule formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂w}{∂y} & =(1+\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta )\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +\frac{1}{r}(2r\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta )\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta +2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

question.problem: Given that $w(r,\theta )=r(1+\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta ),$ find $\frac{∂w}{∂y},$ where $(x,y)$ are Cartesian coordinates and $(r,\theta )$ are the corresponding plane polar coordinates.
question.worked_solution:
We will make use of the following chain rule formula:

$$
\frac{∂w}{∂y}=\frac{∂w}{∂r}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +\frac{1}{r}\frac{∂w}{∂\theta }\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta 
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $w$ with respect to $r$ and $\theta :$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂w}{∂r}=1+\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta ,\,\frac{∂w}{∂\theta }=2r\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta \end{aligned}
$$

Then, substituting these into our chain rule formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂w}{∂y} & =(1+\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta )\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +\frac{1}{r}(2r\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta )\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta +2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Question 6
?

Given that w(r,θ)=r(1+sin⁡2θ), find ∂w∂y, where (x,y) are Cartesian coordinates and (r,θ) are the corresponding plane polar coordinates.

a
sin⁡θ+sin⁡θsin⁡2θ+2cos⁡θcos⁡2θ
b
sin⁡θ+cos⁡θsin⁡2θ−2sin⁡θcos⁡2θ
c
sin⁡θsin⁡2θ+2cos⁡θcos⁡2θ
d
sin⁡2θ+sin⁡θsin⁡2θ+2cos⁡θcos⁡2θ
e
cos⁡θ+cos⁡θsin⁡2θ−2sin⁡θcos⁡2θ
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

We will make use of the following chain rule formula:

∂w∂y=∂w∂rsin⁡θ+1r∂w∂θcos⁡θ

First, we find the partial derivatives of w with respect to r and θ:

∂w∂r=1+sin⁡2θ,∂w∂θ=2rcos⁡2θ

Then, substituting these into our chain rule formula, we get

∂w∂y=(1+sin⁡2θ)sin⁡θ+1r(2rcos⁡2θ)cos⁡θ=sin⁡θ+sin⁡θsin⁡2θ+2cos⁡θcos⁡2θ.

First, we find the partial derivatives of $h$ with respect to $r$ and $\theta :$

Then, substituting these into our chain rule formula, we get

$$

Question 7

Given that h(r,θ)=r(cos⁡θ−1), find ∂h∂x, where (x,y) are Cartesian coordinates and (r,θ) are the corresponding plane polar coordinates.

a
−cos⁡θ
b
−sin⁡θ
c
1−sin⁡θ
d
sin⁡θ−cos⁡θ
e
1−cos⁡θ
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

∂h∂x=∂h∂rcos⁡θ−1r∂h∂θsin⁡θ.

First, we find the partial derivatives of h with respect to r and θ:

∂h∂r=cos⁡θ−1,∂h∂θ=−rsin⁡θ

Question 9
?

Given that v(r,θ)=r(2+cos⁡θ), find ∂v∂x, where (x,y) are Cartesian coordinates and (r,θ) are the corresponding plane polar coordinates.

a
2cos⁡θ
b
2sin⁡θ+1
c
2cos⁡θ+1
d
2sin⁡θ−1
e
cos⁡θ+1
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

We will make use of the following chain rule formula:

∂v∂x=∂v∂rcos⁡θ−1r∂v∂θsin⁡θ

First, we find the partial derivatives of v with respect to r and θ:

∂v∂r=2+cos⁡θ,∂v∂θ=−rsin⁡θ

Then, substituting these into our chain rule formula, we get

∂v∂x=(2+cos⁡θ)cos⁡θ−1r(−rsin⁡θ)sin⁡θ=2cos⁡θ+cos2⁡θ+sin2⁡θ=2cos⁡θ+1.

$$
\frac{∂v}{∂x}=\frac{∂v}{∂r}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -\frac{1}{r}\frac{∂v}{∂\theta }\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta 
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $v$ with respect to $r$ and $\theta :$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂v}{∂r}=2r+2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,\frac{∂v}{∂\theta }=-2r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \end{aligned}
$$

Then, substituting these into our chain rule formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂v}{∂x} & =(2r+2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -\frac{1}{r}(-2r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =2r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +2{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +2{sin}^{2}⁡\theta  \\  & =2r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +2({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta ) \\  & =2r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +2.\end{aligned}
$$

Given that v(r,θ)=r2+2rcos⁡θ, find ∂v∂x, where (x,y) are Cartesian coordinates and (r,θ) are the corresponding plane polar coordinates.

a
2rcos⁡θ+2
b
 r(cos⁡θ+1)
c
 rcos⁡θ+2sin⁡θ
d
 r2(cos⁡θ+sin⁡(2θ))
e
 2rcos⁡θ
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

We will make use of the following chain rule formula:

∂v∂x=∂v∂rcos⁡θ−1r∂v∂θsin⁡θ

First, we find the partial derivatives of v with respect to r and θ:

∂v∂r=2r+2cos⁡θ,∂v∂θ=−2rsin⁡θ

Then, substituting these into our chain rule formula, we get

∂v∂x=(2r+2cos⁡θ)cos⁡θ−1r(−2rsin⁡θ)sin⁡θ=2rcos⁡θ+2cos2⁡θ+2sin2⁡θ=2rcos⁡θ+2(cos2⁡θ+sin2⁡θ)=2rcos⁡θ+2.

tutorial.name: The Multivariable Chain Rule With Cylindrical Polar Coordinates
tutorial.problem:
Given a function of three variables $f(x,y,z),$ we can find formulas for $f_r, f_\theta,$ and $f_z,$ where $(r,\theta,z)$ are cylindrical polar coordinates. The results that we need are as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂r} & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\frac{∂f}{∂y}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ \frac{∂f}{∂\theta } & =-\frac{∂f}{∂x}r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +\frac{∂f}{∂y}r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ \frac{∂f}{∂z} & =\frac{∂f}{∂z}.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that the first and second equations are identical to the equations derived for plane polar coordinates, as we would expect. 

The difference here is that we now have a third equation that deals with the $z$-dependence. But since the $z$-coordinate is the same in both Cartesian and cylindrical polar coordinates, we can simply differentiate with respect to $z$ as usual.

Let's see an example.

observed_steps.worked_solution:
Applying the multivariable chain rule for the function $w(x,y,z)$ with three independent variables $r, \theta,$ and $z,$ where $x=r\cos\theta, y=r\sin\theta,$ and $z=z,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂w}{∂\theta } & =\frac{∂w}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂\theta }+\frac{∂w}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂\theta }+\frac{∂w}{∂z}\cdot \frac{∂z}{∂\theta } \\  & =-\frac{∂w}{∂x}r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +\frac{∂w}{∂y}r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $w$ with respect to $x$ and $y{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂w}{∂x}=2x{z}^{3},\,\frac{∂w}{∂y}=4y{z}^{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $r, \theta,$ and $z,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂w}{∂x} & =2r{z}^{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta , \\ \frac{∂w}{∂y} & =4r{z}^{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting these into our chain rule formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂w}{∂\theta } & =-(2r{z}^{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +(4r{z}^{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =-2{r}^{2}{z}^{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +4{r}^{2}{z}^{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =2{r}^{2}{z}^{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & ={r}^{2}{z}^{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

question.problem: Given that $w(x,y,z)=z^3(x^2+2y^2),$ find $\dfrac{\partial w}{\partial \theta},$ where $(x,y,z)$ are Cartesian coordinates and $(r,\theta,z)$ are the corresponding cylindrical polar coordinates.
question.worked_solution:
Applying the multivariable chain rule for the function $w(x,y,z)$ with three independent variables $r, \theta,$ and $z,$ where $x=r\cos\theta, y=r\sin\theta,$ and $z=z,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂w}{∂\theta } & =\frac{∂w}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂\theta }+\frac{∂w}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂\theta }+\frac{∂w}{∂z}\cdot \frac{∂z}{∂\theta } \\  & =-\frac{∂w}{∂x}r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +\frac{∂w}{∂y}r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $w$ with respect to $x$ and $y{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂w}{∂x}=2x{z}^{3},\,\frac{∂w}{∂y}=4y{z}^{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $r, \theta,$ and $z,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂w}{∂x} & =2r{z}^{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta , \\ \frac{∂w}{∂y} & =4r{z}^{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting these into our chain rule formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂w}{∂\theta } & =-(2r{z}^{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +(4r{z}^{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =-2{r}^{2}{z}^{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +4{r}^{2}{z}^{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =2{r}^{2}{z}^{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & ={r}^{2}{z}^{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Question 11
?

Given that g(x,y,z)=x2z+z2, find ∂g∂z, where (x,y,z) are Cartesian coordinates and (r,θ,z) are the corresponding cylindrical polar coordinates.

a
r2cos2⁡θ+2z
b
r2sin2⁡θ+z
c
2rcos⁡2θ+2z
d
2rsin⁡2θ+z
e
cos2⁡θ+2rz
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Applying the multivariable chain rule for the function g(x,y,z) with three independent variables r,θ, and z, where x=rcos⁡θ,y=rsin⁡θ, and z=z, we have

∂g∂z=∂g∂x⋅∂x∂z+∂g∂y⋅∂y∂z+∂g∂z⋅∂z∂z=∂g∂z.

First, we find the partial derivatives of g with respect to z:

∂g∂z=x2+2z

Writing the above results in terms of r,θ, and z, we get

∂g∂z=r2cos2⁡θ+2z.

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂w}{∂x}={z}^{4},\,\frac{∂w}{∂y}=1\end{aligned}

$$

$$

Question 12

Given that w(x,y,z)=xz4+y, find ∂w∂r, where (x,y,z) are Cartesian coordinates and (r,θ,z) are the corresponding cylindrical polar coordinates.

a
z4cos⁡θ+sin⁡θ
b
r4cos⁡θ−sin⁡2θ
c
cos⁡θ+sin⁡θ
d
z4sin⁡θ+cos⁡θ
e
cos2⁡θ+z4sin2⁡θ
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Applying the multivariable chain rule for the function w(x,y,z) with three independent variables r,θ, and z, where x=rcos⁡θ,y=rsin⁡θ, and z=z, we have

∂w∂r=∂w∂x⋅∂x∂r+∂w∂y⋅∂y∂r+∂w∂z⋅∂z∂r=∂w∂xcos⁡θ+∂w∂ysin⁡θ.

First, we find the partial derivatives of w with respect to x and y:

∂w∂x=z4,∂w∂y=1

Writing the above results in terms of r,θ, and z, we get

∂w∂x=z4,∂w∂y=1.

Finally, substituting these into our chain rule formula, we get ∂w∂r=(z4)cos⁡θ+(1)sin⁡θ=z4cos⁡θ+sin⁡θ.

Question 13
?

Given that h(x,y,z)=xyz, find ∂h∂θ, where (x,y,z) are Cartesian coordinates and (r,θ,z) are the corresponding cylindrical polar coordinates.

a
r2z
b
2rzcos⁡2θ
c
rzcos2⁡θ
d
r2zcos⁡2θ
e
r2zsin⁡2θ
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Applying the multivariable chain rule for the function h(x,y,z) with three independent variables r,θ, and z, where x=rcos⁡θ,y=rsin⁡θ, and z=z, we have

∂h∂θ=∂h∂x⋅∂x∂θ+∂h∂y⋅∂y∂θ+∂h∂z⋅∂z∂θ=−∂h∂xrsin⁡θ+∂h∂yrcos⁡θ.

First, we find the partial derivatives of h with respect to x and y:

∂h∂x=yz,∂h∂y=xz

Writing the above results in terms of r,θ, and z, we get

∂h∂x=rzsin⁡θ,∂h∂y=rzcos⁡θ.

Finally, substituting these into our chain rule formula, we get

∂h∂θ=−(rzsin⁡θ)rsin⁡θ+(rzcos⁡θ)rcos⁡θ=−r2zsin2⁡θ+r2zcos2⁡θ=r2z(cos2⁡θ−sin2⁡θ)=r2zcos⁡2θ.

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=2x,\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=3{y}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $r,\theta ,$ and $z,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =2r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta , \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =3{r}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}

Finally, substituting these into our chain rule formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂r} & =(2r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +(3{r}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =2r{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +3{r}^{2}{sin}^{3}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 14
?

Given that f(x,y,z)=x2+y3+z4, find ∂f∂r, where (x,y,z) are Cartesian coordinates and (r,θ,z) are the corresponding cylindrical polar coordinates.

a
2rcos⁡θ+r3sin3⁡θ
b
2rcos⁡θ+r2sin4⁡θ
c
2rcos⁡(2θ)+3r3sin⁡(4θ)
d
rcos2⁡θ+r3sin4⁡θ
e
2rcos2⁡θ+3r2sin3⁡θ
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Applying the multivariable chain rule for the function f(x,y,z) with three independent variables r,θ, and z, where x=rcos⁡θ,y=rsin⁡θ, and z=z, we have

∂f∂r=∂f∂x⋅∂x∂r+∂f∂y⋅∂y∂r+∂f∂z⋅∂z∂r=∂f∂xcos⁡θ+∂f∂ysin⁡θ.

First, we find the partial derivatives of f with respect to x and y:

∂f∂x=2x,∂f∂y=3y2

Writing the above results in terms of r,θ, and z, we get

∂f∂x=2rcos⁡θ,∂f∂y=3r2sin2⁡θ.

Finally, substituting these into our chain rule formula, we get ∂f∂r=(2rcos⁡θ)cos⁡θ+(3r2sin2⁡θ)sin⁡θ=2rcos2⁡θ+3r2sin3⁡θ.

$$

question.html:
Question 15
?

Given that f(x,y,z)=xyz2, find ∂f∂z, where (x,y,z) are Cartesian coordinates and (r,θ,z) are the corresponding cylindrical polar coordinates.

a
 2rzsin⁡(2θ)
b
 rzsin⁡θ
c
 zsin⁡(2θ)
d
 r2zcos2⁡θ
e
 r2zsin⁡(2θ)
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Applying the multivariable chain rule for the function f(x,y,z) with three independent variables r,θ, and z, where x=rcos⁡θ,y=rsin⁡θ, and z=z, we have

∂f∂z=∂f∂x⋅∂x∂z+∂f∂y⋅∂y∂z+∂f∂z⋅∂z∂z=∂f∂z.

First, we find the partial derivatives of f with respect to z:

∂f∂z=2xyz

Writing the above results in terms of r,θ, and z, we get

∂f∂z=2r2zsin⁡θcos⁡θ=r2zsin⁡(2θ).

tutorial.name: The Multivariable Chain Rule With Spherical Polar Coordinates
tutorial.problem:
Suppose that we have a function $f(x,y,z),$ and we wish to find formulas for $f_\rho,$ $f_\theta,$ and $f_\phi$, where $(\rho,\theta,\phi)$ are spherical polar coordinates.

Using the multivariable chain rule, it can be shown that

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂\rho } & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ+\frac{∂f}{∂z}\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂\theta } & =-\frac{∂f}{∂x}\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂ϕ} & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ-\frac{∂f}{∂z}\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ.\end{aligned}
$$

You might want to try deriving these formulas for yourself!

question.name: Question 1
question.problem: Given that $f(x,y)=2y-xy,$ find $\frac{∂f}{∂\theta },$ where $(x,y)$ are Cartesian coordinates and $(r,\theta )$ are the corresponding plane polar coordinates.
question.worked_solution:
Applying the multivariable chain rule for the function $f(x,y)$ with two independent variables $r$ and $\theta ,$ where $x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ and $y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂\theta } & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂\theta }+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂\theta } \\  & =-\frac{∂f}{∂x}r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +\frac{∂f}{∂y}r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=-y,\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=2-x\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $r$ and $\theta ,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =-r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta , \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =2-r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting these into our chain rule formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂\theta } & =(-r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,(-r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )+(2-r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & ={r}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta +2r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -{r}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta  \\  & ={r}^{2}({sin}^{2}⁡\theta -{cos}^{2}⁡\theta )+2r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =-{r}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta )+2r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =2r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -{r}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta ).\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 1
?

Given that f(x,y)=2y−xy, find ∂f∂θ, where (x,y) are Cartesian coordinates and (r,θ) are the corresponding plane polar coordinates.

a
 2rsin⁡θ−rcos⁡θ
b
 r2(cos⁡θ+sin⁡(2θ))
c
2rcos⁡θ−r2cos⁡(2θ)
d
 r(sin⁡θ+cos⁡(2θ))
e
 cos⁡θ−r2sin⁡(2θ)
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Applying the multivariable chain rule for the function f(x,y) with two independent variables r and θ, where x=rcos⁡θ and y=rsin⁡θ, we have

∂f∂θ=∂f∂x⋅∂x∂θ+∂f∂y⋅∂y∂θ=−∂f∂xrsin⁡θ+∂f∂yrcos⁡θ.

First, we find the partial derivatives of f with respect to x and y: ∂f∂x=−y,∂f∂y=2−x

Writing the above results in terms of r and θ, we get

∂f∂x=−rsin⁡θ,∂f∂y=2−rcos⁡θ.

Finally, substituting these into our chain rule formula, we get ∂f∂θ=(−rsin⁡θ)(−rsin⁡θ)+(2−rcos⁡θ)rcos⁡θ=r2sin2⁡θ+2rcos⁡θ−r2cos2⁡θ=r2(sin2⁡θ−cos2⁡θ)+2rcos⁡θ=−r2cos⁡(2θ)+2rcos⁡θ=2rcos⁡θ−r2cos⁡(2θ).

last_observation.worked_solution:
Applying the multivariable chain rule for the function $f(x,y)$ with two independent variables $r$ and $\theta ,$ where $x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ and $y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂\theta } & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂\theta }+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂\theta } \\  & =-\frac{∂f}{∂x}r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +\frac{∂f}{∂y}r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=-y,\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=2-x\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $r$ and $\theta ,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =-r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta , \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =2-r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting these into our chain rule formula, we get

$$

$$

question.html:
Question 1
?

Given that f(x,y)=2y−xy, find ∂f∂θ, where (x,y) are Cartesian coordinates and (r,θ) are the corresponding plane polar coordinates.

a
 2rsin⁡θ−rcos⁡θ
b
 r2(cos⁡θ+sin⁡(2θ))
c
2rcos⁡θ−r2cos⁡(2θ)
d
 r(sin⁡θ+cos⁡(2θ))
e
 cos⁡θ−r2sin⁡(2θ)
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Applying the multivariable chain rule for the function f(x,y) with two independent variables r and θ, where x=rcos⁡θ and y=rsin⁡θ, we have

∂f∂θ=∂f∂x⋅∂x∂θ+∂f∂y⋅∂y∂θ=−∂f∂xrsin⁡θ+∂f∂yrcos⁡θ.

First, we find the partial derivatives of f with respect to x and y: ∂f∂x=−y,∂f∂y=2−x

Writing the above results in terms of r and θ, we get

∂f∂x=−rsin⁡θ,∂f∂y=2−rcos⁡θ.

Finally, substituting these into our chain rule formula, we get ∂f∂θ=(−rsin⁡θ)(−rsin⁡θ)+(2−rcos⁡θ)rcos⁡θ=r2sin2⁡θ+2rcos⁡θ−r2cos2⁡θ=r2(sin2⁡θ−cos2⁡θ)+2rcos⁡θ=−r2cos⁡(2θ)+2rcos⁡θ=2rcos⁡θ−r2cos⁡(2θ).
question.knowledge_point: Calculating the Derivative of a Cartesian Function With Respect to Plane Polar Coordinates

solution.reasoning: Holding r fixed, substitute x=r\cos\theta and y=r\sin\theta to obtain f=2r\sin\theta-r^2\sin\theta\cos\theta. Thus \partial f/\partial\theta=2r\cos\theta-r^2(\cos^2\theta-\sin^2\theta)=2r\cos\theta-r^2\cos(2\theta), which matches option c. Question 1
?

Given that f(x,y)=2y−xy, find ∂f∂θ, where (x,y) are Cartesian coordinates and (r,θ) are the corresponding plane polar coordinates.

a
 2rsin⁡θ−rcos⁡θ
b
 r2(cos⁡θ+sin⁡(2θ))
c
2rcos⁡θ−r2cos⁡(2θ)
d
 r(sin⁡θ+cos⁡(2θ))
e
 cos⁡θ−r2sin⁡(2θ)
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Applying the multivariable chain rule for the function f(x,y) with two independent variables r and θ, where x=rcos⁡θ and y=rsin⁡θ, we have

∂f∂θ=∂f∂x⋅∂x∂θ+∂f∂y⋅∂y∂θ=−∂f∂xrsin⁡θ+∂f∂yrcos⁡θ.

First, we find the partial derivatives of f with respect to x and y: ∂f∂x=−y,∂f∂y=2−x

Writing the above results in terms of r and θ, we get

∂f∂x=−rsin⁡θ,∂f∂y=2−rcos⁡θ.

Finally, substituting these into our chain rule formula, we get ∂f∂θ=(−rsin⁡θ)(−rsin⁡θ)+(2−rcos⁡θ)rcos⁡θ=r2sin2⁡θ+2rcos⁡θ−r2cos2⁡θ=r2(sin2⁡θ−cos2⁡θ)+2rcos⁡θ=−r2cos⁡(2θ)+2rcos⁡θ=2rcos⁡θ−r2cos⁡(2θ).

question.name: Question 2
question.problem: Given that $g(x,y)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y),$ find $\frac{∂g}{∂r},$ where $(x,y)$ are Cartesian coordinates and $(r,\theta )$ are the corresponding plane polar coordinates.
question.worked_solution:
Applying the multivariable chain rule for the function $g(x,y)$ with two independent variables $r$ and $\theta ,$ where $x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ and $y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂g}{∂r} & =\frac{∂g}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂r}+\frac{∂g}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂r} \\  & =\frac{∂g}{∂x}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\frac{∂g}{∂y}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $g$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂g}{∂x}=\frac{1}{x+y},\,\frac{∂g}{∂y}=\frac{1}{x+y}\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $r$ and $\theta ,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂g}{∂x} & =\frac{1}{r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }, \\ \frac{∂g}{∂y} & =\frac{1}{r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting these into our chain rule formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂g}{∂r} & =(\frac{1}{r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta })\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +(\frac{1}{r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta })\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }{r(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )} \\  & =\frac{1}{r}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂g}{∂r} & =\frac{∂g}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂r}+\frac{∂g}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂r} \\  & =\frac{∂g}{∂x}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\frac{∂g}{∂y}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $g$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂g}{∂x}=\frac{1}{x+y},\,\frac{∂g}{∂y}=\frac{1}{x+y}\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $r$ and $\theta ,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂g}{∂x} & =\frac{1}{r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }, \\ \frac{∂g}{∂y} & =\frac{1}{r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting these into our chain rule formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂g}{∂r} & =(\frac{1}{r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta })\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +(\frac{1}{r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta })\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }{r(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )} \\  & =\frac{1}{r}.\end{aligned}
$$

feedback.problem: Given that $g(x,y)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y),$ find $\frac{∂g}{∂r},$ where $(x,y)$ are Cartesian coordinates and $(r,\theta )$ are the corresponding plane polar coordinates.
feedback.worked_solution:
Applying the multivariable chain rule for the function $g(x,y)$ with two independent variables $r$ and $\theta ,$ where $x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ and $y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂g}{∂r} & =\frac{∂g}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂r}+\frac{∂g}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂r} \\  & =\frac{∂g}{∂x}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\frac{∂g}{∂y}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $g$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂g}{∂x}=\frac{1}{x+y},\,\frac{∂g}{∂y}=\frac{1}{x+y}\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $r$ and $\theta ,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂g}{∂x} & =\frac{1}{r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }, \\ \frac{∂g}{∂y} & =\frac{1}{r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting these into our chain rule formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂g}{∂r} & =(\frac{1}{r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta })\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +(\frac{1}{r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta })\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }{r(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )} \\  & =\frac{1}{r}.\end{aligned}
$$

c
cos⁡θ−sin⁡θcos⁡θ+sin⁡θ

Applying the multivariable chain rule for the function g(x,y) with two independent variables r and θ, where x=rcos⁡θ and y=rsin⁡θ, we have

∂g∂r=∂g∂x⋅∂x∂r+∂g∂y⋅∂y∂r=∂g∂xcos⁡θ+∂g∂ysin⁡θ.

First, we find the partial derivatives of g with respect to x and y:

∂g∂x=1x+y,∂g∂y=1x+y

Writing the above results in terms of r and θ, we get

∂g∂x=1rcos⁡θ+rsin⁡θ,∂g∂y=1rcos⁡θ+rsin⁡θ.

Finally, substituting these into our chain rule formula, we get

∂g∂r=(1rcos⁡θ+rsin⁡θ)cos⁡θ+(1rcos⁡θ+rsin⁡θ)sin⁡θ=cos⁡θ+sin⁡θr(cos⁡θ+sin⁡θ)=1r.

question.name: Question 3
question.problem: Given that $h(x,y)={x}^{2}-{y}^{2},$ find $\frac{∂h}{∂r},$ where $(x,y)$ are Cartesian coordinates and $(r,\theta )$ are the corresponding plane polar coordinates.
question.worked_solution:
Applying the multivariable chain rule for the function $h(x,y)$ with two independent variables $r$ and $\theta ,$ where $x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ and $y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂h}{∂r} & =\frac{∂h}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂r}+\frac{∂h}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂r} \\  & =\frac{∂h}{∂x}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\frac{∂h}{∂y}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $h$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂h}{∂x}=2x,\,\frac{∂h}{∂y}=-2y\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $r$ and $\theta ,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂h}{∂x} & =2r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta , \\ \frac{∂h}{∂y} & =-2r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting these into our chain rule formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂h}{∂r} & =(2r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -(2r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =2r({cos}^{2}⁡\theta -{sin}^{2}⁡\theta ) \\  & =2r\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta ).\end{aligned}
$$

Question 3
?

Given that h(x,y)=x2−y2, find ∂h∂r, where (x,y) are Cartesian coordinates and (r,θ) are the corresponding plane polar coordinates.

a
r2cos⁡(2θ)
b
2rsin⁡(2θ)
c
2rsin2⁡θ
d
2rcos2⁡θ
e
2rcos⁡(2θ)
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Applying the multivariable chain rule for the function h(x,y) with two independent variables r and θ, where x=rcos⁡θ and y=rsin⁡θ, we have

∂h∂r=∂h∂x⋅∂x∂r+∂h∂y⋅∂y∂r=∂h∂xcos⁡θ+∂h∂ysin⁡θ.

First, we find the partial derivatives of h with respect to x and y:

∂h∂x=2x,∂h∂y=−2y

Writing the above results in terms of r and θ, we get

∂h∂x=2rcos⁡θ,∂h∂y=−2rsin⁡θ.

Finally, substituting these into our chain rule formula, we get ∂h∂r=(2rcos⁡θ)cos⁡θ−(2rsin⁡θ)sin⁡θ=2r(cos2⁡θ−sin2⁡θ)=2rcos⁡(2θ).

last_observation.worked_solution:
Applying the multivariable chain rule for the function $h(x,y)$ with two independent variables $r$ and $\theta ,$ where $x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ and $y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂h}{∂r} & =\frac{∂h}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂r}+\frac{∂h}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂r} \\  & =\frac{∂h}{∂x}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\frac{∂h}{∂y}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $h$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂h}{∂x}=2x,\,\frac{∂h}{∂y}=-2y\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $r$ and $\theta ,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂h}{∂x} & =2r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta , \\ \frac{∂h}{∂y} & =-2r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting these into our chain rule formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂h}{∂r} & =(2r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -(2r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =2r({cos}^{2}⁡\theta -{sin}^{2}⁡\theta ) \\  & =2r\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta ).\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂h}{∂x}=2x,\,\frac{∂h}{∂y}=-2y\end{aligned}

Writing the above results in terms of $r$ and $\theta ,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂h}{∂x} & =2r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta , \\ \frac{∂h}{∂y} & =-2r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}

question.html:
Question 3
?

Given that h(x,y)=x2−y2, find ∂h∂r, where (x,y) are Cartesian coordinates and (r,θ) are the corresponding plane polar coordinates.

a
r2cos⁡(2θ)
b
2rsin⁡(2θ)
c
2rsin2⁡θ
d
2rcos2⁡θ
e
2rcos⁡(2θ)
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Applying the multivariable chain rule for the function h(x,y) with two independent variables r and θ, where x=rcos⁡θ and y=rsin⁡θ, we have

∂h∂r=∂h∂x⋅∂x∂r+∂h∂y⋅∂y∂r=∂h∂xcos⁡θ+∂h∂ysin⁡θ.

First, we find the partial derivatives of h with respect to x and y:

∂h∂x=2x,∂h∂y=−2y

Writing the above results in terms of r and θ, we get

∂h∂x=2rcos⁡θ,∂h∂y=−2rsin⁡θ.

Finally, substituting these into our chain rule formula, we get ∂h∂r=(2rcos⁡θ)cos⁡θ−(2rsin⁡θ)sin⁡θ=2r(cos2⁡θ−sin2⁡θ)=2rcos⁡(2θ).

solution.reasoning: Substituting x=r\cos\theta and y=r\sin\theta gives h=r^2(\cos^2\theta-\sin^2\theta)=r^2\cos(2\theta). Holding \theta fixed, \partial h/\partial r=2r\cos(2\theta), matching option e. No Math Academy answer or grade is captured for this question; the worked example concerns a different function.

Question 3

Given that h(x,y)=x2−y2, find ∂h∂r, where (x,y) are Cartesian coordinates and (r,θ) are the corresponding plane polar coordinates.

a
r2cos⁡(2θ)
b
2rsin⁡(2θ)
c
2rsin2⁡θ
d
2rcos2⁡θ
e
2rcos⁡(2θ)
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Applying the multivariable chain rule for the function h(x,y) with two independent variables r and θ, where x=rcos⁡θ and y=rsin⁡θ, we have

∂h∂r=∂h∂x⋅∂x∂r+∂h∂y⋅∂y∂r=∂h∂xcos⁡θ+∂h∂ysin⁡θ.

First, we find the partial derivatives of h with respect to x and y:

∂h∂x=2x,∂h∂y=−2y

Writing the above results in terms of r and θ, we get

∂h∂x=2rcos⁡θ,∂h∂y=−2rsin⁡θ.

Finally, substituting these into our chain rule formula, we get ∂h∂r=(2rcos⁡θ)cos⁡θ−(2rsin⁡θ)sin⁡θ=2r(cos2⁡θ−sin2⁡θ)=2rcos⁡(2θ).

question.problem: Given that $p(x,y)=2x+{y}^{2},$ find $\frac{∂p}{∂\theta },$ where $(x,y)$ are Cartesian coordinates and $(r,\theta )$ are the corresponding plane polar coordinates.
question.worked_solution:
Applying the multivariable chain rule for the function $p(x,y)$ with two independent variables $r$ and $\theta ,$ where $x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ and $y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂p}{∂\theta } & =\frac{∂p}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂\theta }+\frac{∂p}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂\theta } \\  & =-\frac{∂p}{∂x}r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +\frac{∂p}{∂y}r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $n$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂p}{∂x}=2,\,\frac{∂p}{∂y}=2y\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $r$ and $\theta ,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂p}{∂x} & =2, \\ \frac{∂p}{∂y} & =2r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting these into our chain rule formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂p}{∂\theta } & =-2r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +(2r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =-2r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +2{r}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & ={r}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )-2r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂p}{∂\theta } & =\frac{∂p}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂\theta }+\frac{∂p}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂\theta } \\  & =-\frac{∂p}{∂x}r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +\frac{∂p}{∂y}r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $n$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂p}{∂x}=2,\,\frac{∂p}{∂y}=2y\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $r$ and $\theta ,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂p}{∂x} & =2, \\ \frac{∂p}{∂y} & =2r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting these into our chain rule formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂p}{∂\theta } & =-2r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +(2r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =-2r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +2{r}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & ={r}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )-2r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Question 4
?

Given that p(x,y)=2x+y2, find ∂p∂θ, where (x,y) are Cartesian coordinates and (r,θ) are the corresponding plane polar coordinates.

a
r2sin⁡(2θ)
b
r2sin⁡(2θ)−2rsin⁡θ
c
r2sin2⁡θ−2rcos⁡θ
d
−2r2sin⁡(2θ)+rsin⁡θ
e
−2r2cos⁡θ
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Applying the multivariable chain rule for the function p(x,y) with two independent variables r and θ, where x=rcos⁡θ and y=rsin⁡θ, we have

∂p∂θ=∂p∂x⋅∂x∂θ+∂p∂y⋅∂y∂θ=−∂p∂xrsin⁡θ+∂p∂yrcos⁡θ.

First, we find the partial derivatives of n with respect to x and y: ∂p∂x=2,∂p∂y=2y

Writing the above results in terms of r and θ, we get

∂p∂x=2,∂p∂y=2rsin⁡θ.

Finally, substituting these into our chain rule formula, we get ∂p∂θ=−2rsin⁡θ+(2rsin⁡θ)rcos⁡θ=−2rsin⁡θ+2r2sin⁡θcos⁡θ=r2sin⁡(2θ)−2rsin⁡θ.

solution.reasoning: Substituting x=r\cos\theta and y=r\sin\theta gives p=2r\cos\theta+r^2\sin^2\theta. Holding r fixed, \partial p/\partial\theta=-2r\sin\theta+2r^2\sin\theta\cos\theta=r^2\sin(2\theta)-2r\sin\theta, matching option b. feedback.name: Question 4
feedback.problem: Given that $p(x,y)=2x+{y}^{2},$ find $\frac{∂p}{∂\theta },$ where $(x,y)$ are Cartesian coordinates and $(r,\theta )$ are the corresponding plane polar coordinates.
feedback.worked_solution:
Applying the multivariable chain rule for the function $p(x,y)$ with two independent variables $r$ and $\theta ,$ where $x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ and $y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂p}{∂\theta } & =\frac{∂p}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂\theta }+\frac{∂p}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂\theta } \\  & =-\frac{∂p}{∂x}r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +\frac{∂p}{∂y}r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $n$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂p}{∂x}=2,\,\frac{∂p}{∂y}=2y\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $r$ and $\theta ,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂p}{∂x} & =2, \\ \frac{∂p}{∂y} & =2r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting these into our chain rule formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂p}{∂\theta } & =-2r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +(2r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =-2r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +2{r}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & ={r}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )-2r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 5
question.problem: Given that $f(x,y)={x}^{2}+y,$ find $\frac{∂f}{∂\theta },$ where $(x,y)$ are Cartesian coordinates and $(r,\theta )$ are the corresponding plane polar coordinates.
question.worked_solution:
Applying the multivariable chain rule for the function $f(x,y)$ with two independent variables $r$ and $\theta ,$ where $x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ and $y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂\theta } & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂\theta }+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂\theta } \\  & =-\frac{∂f}{∂x}r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +\frac{∂f}{∂y}r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=2x,\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=1\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $r$ and $\theta ,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =2r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta , \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting these into our chain rule formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂\theta } & =-2r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =-{r}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )+r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -{r}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta ).\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 5
?

Given that f(x,y)=x2+y, find ∂f∂θ, where (x,y) are Cartesian coordinates and (r,θ) are the corresponding plane polar coordinates.

a
 r(sin⁡(2θ)+rcos⁡(θ)
b
 rcos⁡θ+rsin⁡(2θ)
c
rcos⁡θ−r2sin⁡(2θ)
d
 r2(cos⁡θ−sin⁡θ)
e
 rsin⁡θ+r2sin⁡(2θ)
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Applying the multivariable chain rule for the function f(x,y) with two independent variables r and θ, where x=rcos⁡θ and y=rsin⁡θ, we have

∂f∂θ=∂f∂x⋅∂x∂θ+∂f∂y⋅∂y∂θ=−∂f∂xrsin⁡θ+∂f∂yrcos⁡θ.

First, we find the partial derivatives of f with respect to x and y: ∂f∂x=2x,∂f∂y=1

Writing the above results in terms of r and θ, we get

∂f∂x=2rcos⁡θ,∂f∂y=1.

Finally, substituting these into our chain rule formula, we get ∂f∂θ=−2rcos⁡θrsin⁡θ+rcos⁡θ=−r2sin⁡(2θ)+rcos⁡θ=rcos⁡θ−r2sin⁡(2θ).

last_observation.worked_solution:
Applying the multivariable chain rule for the function $f(x,y)$ with two independent variables $r$ and $\theta ,$ where $x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ and $y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂\theta } & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂\theta }+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂\theta } \\  & =-\frac{∂f}{∂x}r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +\frac{∂f}{∂y}r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=2x,\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=1\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $r$ and $\theta ,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =2r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta , \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting these into our chain rule formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂\theta } & =-2r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =-{r}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )+r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -{r}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta ).\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 5
?

Given that f(x,y)=x2+y, find ∂f∂θ, where (x,y) are Cartesian coordinates and (r,θ) are the corresponding plane polar coordinates.

a
 r(sin⁡(2θ)+rcos⁡(θ)
b
 rcos⁡θ+rsin⁡(2θ)
c
rcos⁡θ−r2sin⁡(2θ)
d
 r2(cos⁡θ−sin⁡θ)
e
 rsin⁡θ+r2sin⁡(2θ)
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Applying the multivariable chain rule for the function f(x,y) with two independent variables r and θ, where x=rcos⁡θ and y=rsin⁡θ, we have

∂f∂θ=∂f∂x⋅∂x∂θ+∂f∂y⋅∂y∂θ=−∂f∂xrsin⁡θ+∂f∂yrcos⁡θ.

First, we find the partial derivatives of f with respect to x and y: ∂f∂x=2x,∂f∂y=1

Writing the above results in terms of r and θ, we get

∂f∂x=2rcos⁡θ,∂f∂y=1.

Finally, substituting these into our chain rule formula, we get ∂f∂θ=−2rcos⁡θrsin⁡θ+rcos⁡θ=−r2sin⁡(2θ)+rcos⁡θ=rcos⁡θ−r2sin⁡(2θ).

solution.reasoning: Substituting x=r\cos\theta and y=r\sin\theta gives f=r^2\cos^2\theta+r\sin\theta. Holding r fixed, \partial f/\partial\theta=-2r^2\sin\theta\cos\theta+r\cos\theta=r\cos\theta-r^2\sin(2\theta), matching option c. $$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂\theta } & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂\theta }+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂\theta } \\  & =-\frac{∂f}{∂x}r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +\frac{∂f}{∂y}r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=2x,\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=1\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $r$ and $\theta ,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =2r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta , \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting these into our chain rule formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂\theta } & =-2r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =-{r}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )+r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -{r}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta ).\end{aligned}
$$

Question 5
?

Given that f(x,y)=x2+y, find ∂f∂θ, where (x,y) are Cartesian coordinates and (r,θ) are the corresponding plane polar coordinates.

a
 r(sin⁡(2θ)+rcos⁡(θ)
b
 rcos⁡θ+rsin⁡(2θ)
c
rcos⁡θ−r2sin⁡(2θ)
d
 r2(cos⁡θ−sin⁡θ)
e
 rsin⁡θ+r2sin⁡(2θ)
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Applying the multivariable chain rule for the function f(x,y) with two independent variables r and θ, where x=rcos⁡θ and y=rsin⁡θ, we have

∂f∂θ=∂f∂x⋅∂x∂θ+∂f∂y⋅∂y∂θ=−∂f∂xrsin⁡θ+∂f∂yrcos⁡θ.

First, we find the partial derivatives of f with respect to x and y: ∂f∂x=2x,∂f∂y=1

Writing the above results in terms of r and θ, we get

∂f∂x=2rcos⁡θ,∂f∂y=1.

Finally, substituting these into our chain rule formula, we get ∂f∂θ=−2rcos⁡θrsin⁡θ+rcos⁡θ=−r2sin⁡(2θ)+rcos⁡θ=rcos⁡θ−r2sin⁡(2θ).

question.name: Question 6
question.problem: Given that $w(r,\theta )=r(1+\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta ),$ find $\frac{∂w}{∂y},$ where $(x,y)$ are Cartesian coordinates and $(r,\theta )$ are the corresponding plane polar coordinates.
question.worked_solution:
We will make use of the following chain rule formula:

$$
\frac{∂w}{∂y}=\frac{∂w}{∂r}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +\frac{1}{r}\frac{∂w}{∂\theta }\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta 
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $w$ with respect to $r$ and $\theta :$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂w}{∂r}=1+\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta ,\,\frac{∂w}{∂\theta }=2r\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta \end{aligned}
$$

Then, substituting these into our chain rule formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂w}{∂y} & =(1+\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta )\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +\frac{1}{r}(2r\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta )\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta +2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Question 6
?

Given that w(r,θ)=r(1+sin⁡2θ), find ∂w∂y, where (x,y) are Cartesian coordinates and (r,θ) are the corresponding plane polar coordinates.

a
sin⁡θ+sin⁡θsin⁡2θ+2cos⁡θcos⁡2θ
b
sin⁡θ+cos⁡θsin⁡2θ−2sin⁡θcos⁡2θ
c
sin⁡θsin⁡2θ+2cos⁡θcos⁡2θ
d
sin⁡2θ+sin⁡θsin⁡2θ+2cos⁡θcos⁡2θ
e
cos⁡θ+cos⁡θsin⁡2θ−2sin⁡θcos⁡2θ
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

We will make use of the following chain rule formula:

∂w∂y=∂w∂rsin⁡θ+1r∂w∂θcos⁡θ

First, we find the partial derivatives of w with respect to r and θ:

∂w∂r=1+sin⁡2θ,∂w∂θ=2rcos⁡2θ

Then, substituting these into our chain rule formula, we get

∂w∂y=(1+sin⁡2θ)sin⁡θ+1r(2rcos⁡2θ)cos⁡θ=sin⁡θ+sin⁡θsin⁡2θ+2cos⁡θcos⁡2θ.

last_observation.worked_solution:
We will make use of the following chain rule formula:

$$
\frac{∂w}{∂y}=\frac{∂w}{∂r}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +\frac{1}{r}\frac{∂w}{∂\theta }\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta 
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $w$ with respect to $r$ and $\theta :$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂w}{∂r}=1+\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta ,\,\frac{∂w}{∂\theta }=2r\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta \end{aligned}
$$

Then, substituting these into our chain rule formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂w}{∂y} & =(1+\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta )\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +\frac{1}{r}(2r\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta )\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta +2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Question 6
?

Given that w(r,θ)=r(1+sin⁡2θ), find ∂w∂y, where (x,y) are Cartesian coordinates and (r,θ) are the corresponding plane polar coordinates.

a
sin⁡θ+sin⁡θsin⁡2θ+2cos⁡θcos⁡2θ
b
sin⁡θ+cos⁡θsin⁡2θ−2sin⁡θcos⁡2θ
c
sin⁡θsin⁡2θ+2cos⁡θcos⁡2θ
d
sin⁡2θ+sin⁡θsin⁡2θ+2cos⁡θcos⁡2θ
e
cos⁡θ+cos⁡θsin⁡2θ−2sin⁡θcos⁡2θ
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

We will make use of the following chain rule formula:

∂w∂y=∂w∂rsin⁡θ+1r∂w∂θcos⁡θ

First, we find the partial derivatives of w with respect to r and θ:

∂w∂r=1+sin⁡2θ,∂w∂θ=2rcos⁡2θ

Then, substituting these into our chain rule formula, we get

∂w∂y=(1+sin⁡2θ)sin⁡θ+1r(2rcos⁡2θ)cos⁡θ=sin⁡θ+sin⁡θsin⁡2θ+2cos⁡θcos⁡2θ.
question.knowledge_point: Calculating the Derivative of a Polar Function With Respect to Cartesian Coordinates

solution.reasoning: For r>0, the chain rule gives \partial w/\partial y=w_r\sin\theta+(w_\theta/r)\cos\theta. Here w_r=1+\sin(2\theta) and w_\theta=2r\cos(2\theta), so \partial w/\partial y=\sin\theta+\sin\theta\sin(2\theta)+2\cos\theta\cos(2\theta), matching option a. No Math Academy answer or grade is captured for this question; the worked example concerns a different function and derivative.

feedback.name: Question 6
feedback.problem: Given that $w(r,\theta )=r(1+\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta ),$ find $\frac{∂w}{∂y},$ where $(x,y)$ are Cartesian coordinates and $(r,\theta )$ are the corresponding plane polar coordinates.
feedback.worked_solution:
We will make use of the following chain rule formula:

$$
\frac{∂w}{∂y}=\frac{∂w}{∂r}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +\frac{1}{r}\frac{∂w}{∂\theta }\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta 
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $w$ with respect to $r$ and $\theta :$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂w}{∂r}=1+\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta ,\,\frac{∂w}{∂\theta }=2r\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta \end{aligned}
$$

Then, substituting these into our chain rule formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂w}{∂y} & =(1+\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta )\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +\frac{1}{r}(2r\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta )\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta +2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Thus \partial h/\partial x=h_r\cos\theta-(h_\theta/r)\sin\theta=\cos^2\theta-\cos\theta+\sin^2\theta=1-\cos\theta, matching option e. feedback.name: Question 7
feedback.problem: Given that $h(r,\theta )=r(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -1),$ find $\frac{∂h}{∂x},$ where $(x,y)$ are Cartesian coordinates and $(r,\theta )$ are the corresponding plane polar coordinates.
feedback.worked_solution:
We will make use of the following chain rule formula:

$$
\frac{∂h}{∂x}=\frac{∂h}{∂r}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -\frac{1}{r}\frac{∂h}{∂\theta }\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $h$ with respect to $r$ and $\theta :$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂h}{∂r}=\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -1,\,\frac{∂h}{∂\theta }=-r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \end{aligned}
$$

Then, substituting these into our chain rule formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂h}{∂x} & =(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -1)\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -\frac{1}{r}(-r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & ={cos}^{2}⁡\theta -\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta  \\  & =1-\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Question 7
?

Given that h(r,θ)=r(cos⁡θ−1), find ∂h∂x, where (x,y) are Cartesian coordinates and (r,θ) are the corresponding plane polar coordinates.

a
−cos⁡θ
b
−sin⁡θ
c
1−sin⁡θ
d
sin⁡θ−cos⁡θ
e
1−cos⁡θ
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

We will make use of the following chain rule formula:

∂h∂x=∂h∂rcos⁡θ−1r∂h∂θsin⁡θ.

First, we find the partial derivatives of h with respect to r and θ:

∂h∂r=cos⁡θ−1,∂h∂θ=−rsin⁡θ

Then, substituting these into our chain rule formula, we get

∂h∂x=(cos⁡θ−1)cos⁡θ−1r(−rsin⁡θ)sin⁡θ=cos2⁡θ−cos⁡θ+sin2⁡θ=1−cos⁡θ.

question.name: Question 8
question.problem: Given that $v(r,\theta )=r(1+\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta ),$ find $\frac{∂v}{∂y},$ where $(x,y)$ are Cartesian coordinates and $(r,\theta )$ are the corresponding plane polar coordinates.
question.worked_solution:
We will make use of the following chain rule formula:

$$
\frac{∂v}{∂y}=\frac{∂v}{∂r}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +\frac{1}{r}\frac{∂v}{∂\theta }\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $v$ with respect to $r$ and $\theta :$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂v}{∂r}=1+\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta ,\,\frac{∂v}{∂\theta }=-2r\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta \end{aligned}
$$

Then, substituting these into our chain rule formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂v}{∂y} & =(1+\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta )\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +\frac{1}{r}(-2r\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta )\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta -2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Question 8
?

Given that v(r,θ)=r(1+cos⁡2θ), find ∂v∂y, where (x,y) are Cartesian coordinates and (r,θ) are the corresponding plane polar coordinates.

a
sin⁡θ−2cos⁡θsin⁡2θ
b
2sin⁡θcos2⁡θ−cos⁡θsin2⁡θ
c
sin⁡θ+sin⁡θcos⁡2θ−2cos⁡θsin⁡2θ
d
sin⁡θcos⁡2θ−2cos⁡θsin⁡2θ
e
sin⁡θ+cos⁡2θ−2sin⁡2θ
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

We will make use of the following chain rule formula:

∂v∂y=∂v∂rsin⁡θ+1r∂v∂θcos⁡θ.

First, we find the partial derivatives of v with respect to r and θ:

∂v∂r=1+cos⁡2θ,∂v∂θ=−2rsin⁡2θ

Then, substituting these into our chain rule formula, we get

∂v∂y=(1+cos⁡2θ)sin⁡θ+1r(−2rsin⁡2θ)cos⁡θ=sin⁡θ+sin⁡θcos⁡2θ−2cos⁡θsin⁡2θ.

$$
\frac{∂v}{∂y}=\frac{∂v}{∂r}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +\frac{1}{r}\frac{∂v}{∂\theta }\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $v$ with respect to $r$ and $\theta :$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂v}{∂r}=1+\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta ,\,\frac{∂v}{∂\theta }=-2r\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta \end{aligned}
$$

Then, substituting these into our chain rule formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂v}{∂y} & =(1+\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta )\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +\frac{1}{r}(-2r\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta )\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta -2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 8
?

Given that v(r,θ)=r(1+cos⁡2θ), find ∂v∂y, where (x,y) are Cartesian coordinates and (r,θ) are the corresponding plane polar coordinates.

a
sin⁡θ−2cos⁡θsin⁡2θ
b
2sin⁡θcos2⁡θ−cos⁡θsin2⁡θ
c
sin⁡θ+sin⁡θcos⁡2θ−2cos⁡θsin⁡2θ
d
sin⁡θcos⁡2θ−2cos⁡θsin⁡2θ
e
sin⁡θ+cos⁡2θ−2sin⁡2θ
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

We will make use of the following chain rule formula:

∂v∂y=∂v∂rsin⁡θ+1r∂v∂θcos⁡θ.

First, we find the partial derivatives of v with respect to r and θ:

∂v∂r=1+cos⁡2θ,∂v∂θ=−2rsin⁡2θ

Then, substituting these into our chain rule formula, we get

∂v∂y=(1+cos⁡2θ)sin⁡θ+1r(−2rsin⁡2θ)cos⁡θ=sin⁡θ+sin⁡θcos⁡2θ−2cos⁡θsin⁡2θ.
question.knowledge_point: Calculating the Derivative of a Polar Function With Respect to Cartesian Coordinates

solution.reasoning: For r>0, \partial v/\partial y=v_r\sin\theta+(v_\theta/r)\cos\theta. Since v_r=1+\cos(2\theta) and v_\theta=-2r\sin(2\theta), the derivative is \sin\theta+\sin\theta\cos(2\theta)-2\cos\theta\sin(2\theta), matching option c. feedback.name: Question 8
feedback.problem: Given that $v(r,\theta )=r(1+\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta ),$ find $\frac{∂v}{∂y},$ where $(x,y)$ are Cartesian coordinates and $(r,\theta )$ are the corresponding plane polar coordinates.
feedback.worked_solution:
We will make use of the following chain rule formula:

$$
\frac{∂v}{∂y}=\frac{∂v}{∂r}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +\frac{1}{r}\frac{∂v}{∂\theta }\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $v$ with respect to $r$ and $\theta :$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂v}{∂r}=1+\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta ,\,\frac{∂v}{∂\theta }=-2r\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta \end{aligned}
$$

Then, substituting these into our chain rule formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂v}{∂y} & =(1+\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta )\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +\frac{1}{r}(-2r\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta )\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta -2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Question 8
?

Given that v(r,θ)=r(1+cos⁡2θ), find ∂v∂y, where (x,y) are Cartesian coordinates and (r,θ) are the corresponding plane polar coordinates.

a
sin⁡θ−2cos⁡θsin⁡2θ
b
2sin⁡θcos2⁡θ−cos⁡θsin2⁡θ
c
sin⁡θ+sin⁡θcos⁡2θ−2cos⁡θsin⁡2θ
d
sin⁡θcos⁡2θ−2cos⁡θsin⁡2θ
e
sin⁡θ+cos⁡2θ−2sin⁡2θ
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

We will make use of the following chain rule formula:

∂v∂y=∂v∂rsin⁡θ+1r∂v∂θcos⁡θ.

First, we find the partial derivatives of v with respect to r and θ:

∂v∂r=1+cos⁡2θ,∂v∂θ=−2rsin⁡2θ

Then, substituting these into our chain rule formula, we get

∂v∂y=(1+cos⁡2θ)sin⁡θ+1r(−2rsin⁡2θ)cos⁡θ=sin⁡θ+sin⁡θcos⁡2θ−2cos⁡θsin⁡2θ.
